articles.title: Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie , maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X , saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman . The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”
Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year .

articles.title: ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.
She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.
Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.
“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.
French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.
The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.
French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”

articles.title: Tech Moves: Microsoft names 2 leaders, loses 1; DoorDash VP departs; BluePill, Glacis get execs
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: — Weiwei Yang has left Microsoft after more than a decade to co-found a startup that is “building the power grid for the AI age,” according to her LinkedIn profile.

Yang was most recently a senior director with Microsoft Research, working on grid technology. Her team built a grid dataset and released small foundation models to help users operate and expand electrical infrastructure.

Yang thanked the community she built at the tech giant, adding, “I hope the relationships and collaborations we’ve built continue well beyond Microsoft, and that we find many new ways to work together.”

— Allie Mellen has joined Microsoft as principal director for security research and threat intelligence. Mellen was previously a principal analyst at Forrester. She also wrote “Code War,” a book that explores cyberattacks as a powerful geopolitical weapon.

In her new role, Mellen said she will lead strategy for protection and threat intelligence, “helping shape what intelligence we produce, how AI can improve its speed and quality, and how we turn that knowledge into better protection for customers.”
— Agility Robotics , the Salem, Ore., company that had its Nasdaq debut earlier this month, has announced three leadership changes:

— Former tech executive Drew Sheriff has been named as CEO and president of the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass . Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing.

“His skill set is the ideal background for charting how we attract customers and how we delight customers in this new age,” Jeff Seely, board chair for the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, told the Seattle Times .
— Microsoft has named Caroline King as director of its Washington state community and philanthropy team, with a focus on advocacy work across housing, affordability and other priority issues.

King is the founder and past CEO of Washington STEM, an organization that coordinates research, advocacy, policy, philanthropy and partnerships to support science, technology, engineering and math education in the state. She most recently served as a leader on the governing body of an international school in Luxembourg.
— Longtime Amazon and Microsoft tech exec Scott Wiltamuth has retired — mostly.

Wiltamuth joined Amazon in 2011 as an AWS vice president overseeing a large organization building developer and management tools. In 2018, he took a seven-month leave for colon cancer treatment. After returning, he sought a director-level position and thanked company leaders for helping him find a better fit. “Their flexibility and creativity enabled me to extend my AWS career,” he said .
Wiltamuth launched his tech career at Microsoft in 1993 and left nearly 19 years later as director of program management for Visual Studio Pro.
He now spends time with his wife and family, traveling, golfing, swimming and reading. “I don’t plan to pursue another full-time operational role,” Wiltamuth said, “but may do some part-time work.”

— Adam Nygate has exited Palo Alto Networks to co-found and lead a stealth startup based in Seattle. He was founder and CEO of Huntr, a platform launched in 2019 where security researchers could submit information on AI and machine learning vulnerabilities. Protect AI acquired Huntr, and Palo Alto Networks later acquired Protect AI.

“Huntr was a bet that open source gets safer when vulnerabilities are visible to the people who can fix them, even when that made life uncomfortable for vendors who’d rather keep things quiet,” Nygate said in a post announcing his career change and impending new baby.
— BluePill , a Seattle-based marketing startup that helps brands predict consumer behavior, has named Mike Weis as chief revenue officer and head of sales.

Weis has 40 years of experience in consumer packaged goods, retail and commerce, beginning his career as a Pacific Northwest leader at Unilever and holding executive positions at Catalina and Quotient Technologies. Recent roles include adviser at Contento2, eGateway Capital and And1 Advisors.

“Beyond the incredible résumé, Mike is one of the kindest, most genuine, and most passionate people I’ve met. Someone who has accomplished so much, yet brings so much humility, curiosity, and energy to every conversation,” said Ankit Dhawan, CEO and founder of BluePill.

— Glacis , a Seattle startup that builds tamper-proof records of AI behavior, has named Caer Mistral Sanders as a technical co-founder. Sanders has launched startups and joins Glacis from Thoughtworks. Before that, she held leadership roles at Wayfair and Onshape. As a teenager, she published a book on mixed-reality control systems and won a world robotics championship.

In a post announcing the new role, Sanders said she has designed medical record systems, researched robot communication, patented cryptographic technology and built widely used AI platforms. “This is the first time in my career I get to bring all of those skills to bear on one problem, and I couldn’t be more excited!” she added.

— The PNW Battery Collaborative has welcomed Jason Demeny as its director of communications. Demeny is a marketing leader whose past employers include Crusoe, Patch, Qualtrics and Apptio. Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.
The nonprofit PNW Battery Collaborative brings together startups, innovators and researchers focused on energy storage.

— Tom Wheeler , former chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has joined the advisory council for Known , a Bellevue, Wash.-based company building accountability infrastructure for autonomous AI. Wheeler led the FCC from 2013 to 2017.
Known, previously called Identity Digital Innovation Labs, spun out of Identity Digital in September.

— Versium has promoted Matthew Baumgartner to vice president of engineering. The Redmond, Wash.-based company provides data and software that help businesses identify potential customers, fill in missing contact information and target their marketing. Baumgartner has been with Versium since 2018.

— Charlie Trillingham has been named communications manager for University of Washington programs in AI and machine learning. He previously served as a marketing and communications lead for the UW Foster School of Business.

articles.title: Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest update on the investigation , ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.
The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.
ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

articles.title: ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.
The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy , the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.
The new products take that approach further:

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.
Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”
Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.
Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.
“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.
The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.
“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year , is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.
Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.
Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.
Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.
Duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the company, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.
Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar , who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the company, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy said Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”

articles.title: Pinehurst Station Posts Anemic Ridership in First Full Month
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: After Sound Transit inaugurated service on September 30, the Pinehurst infill light rail station in North Seattle averaged a measly 1,034 daily boardings in October, according to the agency's ridership dashboard . That makes it the least used station in the entire 1 Line corridor.

The initial figure is below even the low-end ridership modeling that Sound Transit produced, which showed Pinehurst would attract 2,600 to 4,200 boardings daily by the year 2040. Granted, Pinehurst has 14 years to hit its 2040 projection, but it does have a long way to go.

The busiest station, Westlake, averaged more than 17,000 daily boardings in October, and the entire corridor saw just over 155,000 daily boardings across 27 stations. The median 1 Line station has averaged about 4,000 daily boardings.

Pinehurst's October ridership did exceed seven of the 12 stations that serve only the 2 Line, which has also struggled to build ridership momentum on the Eastside. Bellevue's East Main is the least used light rail station in the entire system, with just 487 daily boardings last month.

Pinehurst is sandwiched between two far more popular stations. Northgate averaged nearly 7,500 daily boardings in October, while Shoreline South (just north of Pinehurst) averaged more than 3,600 daily boardings.

Pinehurst is last among 27 stations on the 1 Line – at least so far. A number of transit advocates warned the station's ridership potential was at risk, as the Harrell administration dragged its feet and ran into legal appeal hurdles as it attempted to rezone the neighborhood surrounding the station.

Rezoning the golf-course-oriented, largely single family neighborhood to encourage apartment development has been part of the pitch for Pinehurst Station from the inception of the grassroots campaign that willed the station into existence. While the station has been funded since the 2016 Sound Transit 3 (ST3) ballot measure, the rezones have been mired in the Seattle Process .
Sound Transit CEO recently appeared on KUOW's Soundside program and was interviewed by David Kroman and Libby Denkmann. They brought up the issue of low ridership at Pinehurst Station.

"Both Libby and I actually ride past the station a few times a week. I have to admit we have made a little bit of a game of counting how many people actually get on and off there," Kroman said. "I think we would both agree that it has been pretty sparse, as far as we can tell. You know, when you look out [from the train], all you really see is I-5, a few single-family homes, a golf course. Do you think more could have been done here, both by the City of Seattle and Sound Transit, to prepare for that station to open?"
Constantine did not take the bait, hewing to a 'if you build it, they will come' line for the station, which carried a budget of $240 million.

"Well, I think, along the way, there are stations with a lot of built-in ridership and stations with less ridership that are about mobility for the people who live close," Constantine said. "And some of those stations with less ridership become centers for growth later, right? And I think this is going to be one of those stations."
The agency CEO alluded to the Pinehurst rezone plan working its way through the process, as he noted some other station areas have transitioned from sparsely populated to dense and bustling.

"The City of Seattle is looking at their growth plans around there, their zoning around there, the incentives they can provide around there for people to create housing," Constantine said. "If you look at our stations up and down the line, our new stations, you see apartment buildings, condominiums going up all over the place by the thousands, and that will happen at Pinehurst as well. So I'm absolutely confident that we're going to see increased ridership at that and other similarly situated stations over time."

At the ribbon-cutting ceremony for Pinehurst, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson echoed Constantine's optimism, which acknowledging the delay and expressing resolve to see the rezones though, which she has also sought to augment with her Taller Faster Denser Plan .

"This is not just a station; it is a spark – a spark for long-term transformation in the newly designated Pinehurst-Haller Lake Urban Center, where we will see more homes, shops, services, parks, and walkable streets, all connected to great transit. That's what it's all about," Wilson said. "Sometimes we build transit where lots of density already exists, and sometimes we build transit, and we're able to welcome people around them."

Constantine and Wilson could have a point based on the path some other stations took. Shoreline South managed just 1,020 daily boardings in its first full month of service – very similar to Pinehurst – but it's more than tripled ridership in the two years since. Shoreline North and Mountlake Terrace took a similar course of steady ridership growth. (On the other hand, Lynnwood City Center's ridership has fluctuated widely, but its level is now similar to when it launched, hovering around the 4,000 daily riders mark.)

That said, ridership growth at each of those locations was buoyed by fairly ambitious upzones that had been put in place before the stations opened, which allowed large apartment complexes to come online near the station opening date. Seattle, on the other hand, is playing catch up after pushing the agency to accelerate the infill station opening, while failing to keep rezone plans on course, despite facing some pressure to do so.

In 2023, former Kenmore Councilmember and Sound Transit Board Member Dave Baker criticized Seattle for not rezoning the Pinehurst neighborhood sooner as Mayor Bruce Harrell and other City officials pushed the agency to accelerate the station's opening.

“I’m sorry Mayor Harrell, I’m not trying to throw stones, but it’s just reality that they’ve had the opportunity to increase zoning in the area to make it more transit-friendly, but it’s still not done,” Baker said. “They’ve had since 2015 to fix the zoning, and it’s now 2023 and the zoning has still not been fixed. I would love to see a successful station… and the system to be as functional as it can. Everything else seems to be happening except this one.”

Harrell brushed off the comment and spent the next few years failing to keep his growth plan on schedule or to insulate it from legal appeals, while undercutting his planning department's more ambitious vision.

After kicking around more meager concepts, the City ultimately queued up a rezone for the Pinehurst-Haller Lake Urban Center allowing five- to eight-story apartment buildings and ground-floor retail in several swaths of Pinehurst and some more limited areas of Haller Lake, replacing some broad areas of low-density Neighborhood Residential (NR) zoning. Other NR areas are set to become Lowrise 1 or 2, which would likely be most enticing to townhome builders, based on recent development patterns.

Across the new urban center, OPCD projected its boldest "Alternative 5" rezone would generate about 2,700 additional homes over 20 years. Meanwhile, the City has projected anemic growth without zoning changes, with just 840 additional homes expected over two decades.

Harrell and his predecessor Jenny Durkan also opposed changes to publicly-owned Jackson Park Golf Course, which advocates had proposed could attract more usage if it incorporated other park uses (or even housing ) – instead of remaining exclusively a fenced, fee-for-entry 27-hole golf course. As it stands, the golf course consumes 160 acres next door to the station, interrupting more direct walking routes to reach it.

If the Pinehurst rezone had not been yoked to the City's broader once-per-decade Comprehensive Plan major update, it might have already happened. However, at the time, City officials seemed to deem it expeditious and convenient to piggyback on the outreach and feedback process for the citywide plan, which they originally set out to pass by the end of 2024 to meet state deadlines.
Pinehurst-based organizer Renee Staton, who fought to add the infill station in the first place, said support for rezones has long been strong in the neighborhood.

"There is substantial community support for a rezone and unlike other communities in Seattle, there is no formal opposition effort to rezoning. In fact, many residents are frustrated with how long the station area planning process is taking, considering it started in 2015," Staton wrote in a guest piece in The Urbanist in September.

Staton has pushed Seattle political leaders and officials at the City's Office of Planning and Community Development (OPCD) to complete the rezone work as soon as possible. Alas, 2028 might be the best case scenario.

"I spoke with OPCD on Monday and they are very optimistic that the One Seattle rezone process will start again in mid-2027 (which I hear as early 2028 given budget season and elections). Pinehurst rezone 2028," Staton added in a social media post last week.

Even if zoning were to be put into place, large apartment complexes often take three years or more to go from a permit application to a completed building, assuming builder interest is immediate – which isn't always guaranteed in a neighborhood more or less starting from scratch on urban development. The broader One Seattle rezones will include opening up many other areas of the city, with some more amenity-rich areas likely more attractive to builders.
In other words, significant amounts of development likely won't be arriving in Pinehurst until the 2030s. A botched neighborhood growth plan can be rectified, but it does take time.

articles.title: Seattle Council and Mayor Spar Over Amended Budget
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: The Seattle City Council finalized 2027-2028 budget legislation, weighing amendments Friday and Monday in a two-day marathon that felt at times like it might go off the rails. Throughout, the process highlighted clear tensions between councilmembers as they argued about transparency and fiscal responsibility under the pressure of a ticking clock.

The meetings culminated in a close 4-5 vote on a piece of legislation sponsored by Councilmember Dionne Foster that would have required council to exercise the same fiscal responsibility they had just voted to continue to require of Seattle’s mayor.

Council President Joy Hollingsworth and Councilmembers Bob Kettle, Maritza Rivera, Rob Saka, and Dan Strauss voted against Foster’s bill. The legislation would have required that the council’s ongoing spending not exceed ongoing revenue, a measure that would help prevent future deficits.

“As we passed the balancing requirement for the mayor last year, I think it's important that we are not holding ourselves to a different standard, or to say differently, if a standard is good enough to ask that we are requesting that another branch of government meet it, I believe it's fair that we ask ourselves to fall in line with that same standard,” Foster said.
In their comments before the vote, councilmembers appeared to tie themselves into rhetorical knots trying to express their commitment to fiscal responsibility while voting explicitly against it.
“I don't need a law to do what's right in this situation,” Strauss said. “I don't need a law to tell or an executive order to tell me how to do my job well.”

Strauss went on to complain that the Mayor’s Office has five months to develop their budget proposal whereas the Budget Chair only has five weeks to create the balancing package, a timeline that predates Strauss’s tenure as Budget Chair.

“As council, we need flexibility,” Saka said. “Again, we are the final check on the Executive as this legislative branch, and I think this ordinance, great in intent and purpose in terms of being sustainable – and I support those broader goals – I also think it would voluntarily restrict one of our most sacred constitutional and charter level responsibilities: deciding how public dollars are spent.”
Kettle agreed that flexibility was paramount, above fiscal responsibility.
“We are a co-equal branch, but we are in a disadvantaged position,” Kettle argued.

“I just want to be clear: it is not that I don't want to hold us accountable to ensuring we have balanced budgets years out, but it takes a certain kind of fiscal responsibility that, as I said earlier, I have not seen in council in many years in order to do that. And part of that, at least for this year's budget, this police piece, I'm sorry, the fire piece was really important to do,” Rivera said.

The council could have chosen to include ongoing funding for the Seattle Fire Department’s (SFD) overtime in their budget proposal instead of one-time funds, but that would have required that they make other difficult choices, which they largely chose to avoid.
Hollingsworth opted not to share her reasons behind her “no” vote.

Central Staff’s explanation, in response to a question from Lin about flexibility, that the legislation wouldn’t preclude the council from exercising discretion when necessary didn’t appear to convince councilmembers who were opposed.
Most of the councilmembers who voted against the bill originally ran on platforms calling for fiscal responsibility and budget audits in 2023.

“I am supportive of Councilmember Foster’s bill that would have held the Council to the same standard of fiscal responsibility as the mayor,” Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said in a statement. “While it didn’t pass out of committee, I sincerely hope the Council takes it up again later this week.”
All legislation considered on Monday will receive another vote at the special Full Council meeting on Friday, November 20.
Last Friday’s meeting included two executive sessions, whereas Monday’s meeting lasted for ten-and-a-half hours and included a last-minute presentation from the council’s Central Staff.

While the council’s budget process is always a bit rushed, Budget Chair Dan Strauss scheduled the final budget vote on November 20 instead of the traditional Tuesday before Thanksgiving, peeling away a few valuable days of discussion and error-checking. This year, holding the vote on November 24 would have added the complication of interim Councilmember Debora Juarez losing her voting power as soon as local officials certify election results that day, with Councilmember-Elect Nilu Jenks taking over when that happens. Unlike Juarez, Jenks is expected to vote with the progressive bloc, generally speaking.

Meanwhile, Strauss’s balancing package , introduced at the beginning of November, included new investments and new revenue sources that councilmembers barely had time to learn about and discuss. Strauss’s original intent was to vote on all budget amendments and legislation on Friday alone, significantly curtailing any chance for councilmembers to debate the merits of the proposals, but he was thwarted when a lawsuit filed by the Seattle Firefighters Pension Board required the council to have two substantial executive sessions to discuss the legal ramifications of the budget policies on which they were voting.

In spite of this setback, councilmembers ended up voting yes on most of the budget amendments before them, adding even more spending – most of it one-time – to a balancing package that had already added more than $40 million to Wilson’s original budget proposal. Even Strauss’s proposal to add $150,000 for Ballard holiday lighting and a lit-up Jimothy decoration was approved, albeit by a close vote. Strauss is a long-time Ballard resident.

City Budget Director Aly Pennucci sent a letter to council on November 6, warning them of the pitfalls ahead. While Pennucci praised Strauss for presenting a balancing package that didn’t present a deficit in 2029, she cautioned councilmembers that including so many supposedly “one-time” adds in the budget could easily knock the budget back into deficit territory in the future. Pennucci identified many one-time adds in the balancing package that had originally been requested as ongoing, calculating that those items being included as ongoing expenses instead would have led to a $21.5 million deficit in 2029. If all the one-time adds for 2027 became ongoing commitments, that would lead to a $41 million deficit.

“I heard clearly from many of you over the last two months that you consider ending one-time funding as a ‘budget cut.’ So, I want to be clear with you, City employees, and community partners, that items labeled as ‘one-time’ in the budget for 2027, 2028, or both, will be removed from the 2028 and/or 2029 baseline budget,” Pennucci wrote.

During Monday’s budget meeting, a week and a half after receiving this communication, Councilmember Maritza Rivera said she saw one-time budget adds as a way to potentially prove they should become ongoing.

“Sometimes that means proposing one-time funding with the understanding that that funding might not be ongoing, and we need to hold ourselves accountable for that,” Rivera said. “The hope is that the mayor sees the value of the investments that we include, and that that funding is made ongoing if needed. And of course, there's no guarantees that the mayor will do that.”
Pennucci also warned about Strauss’s diversion of $10 million from the JumpStart reserve, saying if the council didn’t change course, a new reserve policy would need to be developed next year.

“The stated intent of the JumpStart reserve is to protect JumpStart investments against future economic uncertainty, not to fund new Council priorities as it has been used two of the last three years,” Pennucci wrote.

Councilmembers also expressed concern about the adoption of a 0.01% children and families sales tax that was passed by King County earlier this year. Strauss proposed the City take their share of the tax, although he hasn’t developed a long-term spending plan for the usage of this new revenue. In addition, there was a lack of clarity around impacts this action would have on King County’s plans for the money.
“I can't speak fully to what those impacts might be at this time,” said Pennucci.
After Monday’s votes, Wilson released a statement on the council’s budget proposal, pointing out the one-time funding issue.

“The proposal that passed the Select Budget Committee increases spending from the General Fund by a net of $36 million in 2027, $31 million of which is one-time,” Wilson wrote. “ This means that there is over $20 million of Council-proposed spending in 2027 that is not funded in 2028. ” [Emphasis original]
There were a few notable budget amendments and pieces of legislation that did not pass council’s scrutiny, bucking the trend of layering on commitments.

Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck’s proviso on $400,000 in the Seattle Police Department (SPD) until the department implements the three recommendations from the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) regarding their surveillance program was rejected with a 3-6 vote, with Foster and Councilmember Eddie Lin joining Rinck in voting yes.

“I do want to take this opportunity to just say on the record that Axon and Flock are one and the same,” Rinck said just before the vote. “They're companies that have their roots with one another. They have a deep and long history, but they started together. And I don't want us to think that we're necessarily choosing the lesser of two evils. I know Flock has gotten a lot more bad press with the challenges of their system. It's important to note that Axon has a fair share of their own challenges and in fact holds a nearly $32 million contract with ICE.”

In a moment of inadvertent humor before the vote, Saka said he trusted the Mayor’s judgment on this issue. Councilmembers have been overtly critical of Wilson and her judgment for many months, particularly on her decision to pause their surveillance expansion – before she ultimately greenlit it this month after further study.

Strauss’s proviso on $2.5 million of the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) to support bus service on routes 15 and 17 in outer Ballard failed with a 4-5 vote, probably partially motivated by the fact that Route 15 no longer exists and can’t be brought back without a vote from the King County Council.

Finally, Foster’s legislation that would have created a designated fund if and when the City is able to recover the $13.1 million SPD mistakenly paid to its employees earlier this year didn’t receive enough support. The fund would have put aside any recovered funds for affordable housing instead of returning them directly to the General Fund.
Both Saka and Strauss insisted on verbal amendments to Foster’s bill, but even after she agreed to these changes, Strauss abstained, knowing this would mean the bill wouldn’t pass with a 4-4 vote.

Councilmembers had a sudden budget policy decision to make when the Seattle Firefighters Pension Board filed a lawsuit against the City on November 10, as reported by PubliCola . The Board objected to Wilson’s proposal in her budget to eliminate the actuarial account and transfer all of its funds to the statutory pension fund. Wilson had proposed using $10 million of that money for 2027-2028, thus freeing up General Fund money for other purposes.

In his balancing package, Strauss proposed using an additional $22 million of that money over the biennium, freeing up even more General Fund dollars and using up most of the money transferred from the actuarial account, making this another one-time budget fix.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Microsoft’s PAC Failed, but Governor Ferguson Is Still Coming to Heel
articles.author: John Burbank (Guest Contributor)
paras: Two weeks ago, after the blue tsunami buried Trump’s legions and his megacorporate allies, Governor Bob Ferguson convened a session of his newly established Economic Development Council. This wasn’t about taking advantage of this wide-open moment of political opportunity to advance policies for working people in our state. Instead of proposing how to make child care and healthcare affordable and to halt the polarization of wealth and income to the already wealthy and powerful, Ferguson simply signed an executive order to stop all new state regulation of corporate Washington .

The governor was applauded by Brad Smith, President of Microsoft, and Rachel Smith, President of the Washington Roundtable , an advocacy group for big business. It was all smiles at the press conference, but a giveaway to corporate Washington is meaningless to the citizens of our state.

In Washington DC, Microsoft has committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom and the destruction of the East Wing of the White House, plus another $1 million to his inauguration which featured oligarchs including Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, among other anti-patriots.
Was it worth it for Microsoft? Yes. Microsoft received a $144.4 million contract in January from the U.S. Air Force.

Likewise, Amazon has made out well thanks to Trump, with their donation of $5 million for the Ballroom. Amazon Web Services won a Department of Homeland Security cloud contract in June worth up to about $2.6 billion . That’s a return on investment of 52,000%, while Microsoft’s is a measly 1,444%! These corporations are not our friends – they are Trump’s lieutenants for the oligarchy.

Microsoft seems to think it can get away with looking like it is a good corporate citizen, all while building a new political action committee, Washington Needs to Compete . Washington Needs to Compete has nothing to do with competing, but instead focuses on making sure corporate politicians stay in power. Microsoft failed this year. But this PAC has now raised almost $14 million in anticipation of 2027 and 2028 political battles.
They may think they are rich and strategic, but our 2026 election results indicate that they may just be angry about the anti-Trump wave and trying to figure out a way to create an undertow for MAGA.

Washington Needs to Compete spent over $1.7 million to defeat progressive Democrats. But these Democrats prevailed in 5 out of 6 races. In Kitsap County, Washington Needs to Compete spent almost $300,000 to try to defeat Rep. Tarra Simmons, a formerly incarcerated person who worked her way up from prison to law school to becoming an attorney and defending the rights of incarcerated Washingtonians, and who happens to be the best state legislator in running House floor sessions. Simmons won.

Washington Needs to Compete spent over $700,000 to defend Rep. Amy Walen, a car dealer Democrat, who has represented the 48th LD, which is located in the Eastside suburbs and includes Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters. She lost to a progressive Democrat by 5%. While Walen voted against the millionaires tax, her replacement Jessica Forsythe has pledged to support it.

Yes, Washington needs to compete. We need to make our state a place in which workers, including high tech workers and doctors and nurses and professors, want to stay and raise their families. That means we need to compete, not with Alabama, but with Canada.

What makes Canada so great? For a family it is all about making ends meet and thriving. In Canada the parents of a newborn are entitled to over one year of financial support , to enable that infant to be cared for by her parents. In Canada, through government funding, child care costs $10 a day and it is universal. In Washington, child care costs parents ten times as much . In Canada, there are no out-of-pocket costs and no premium for medical services coverage .
At the University of British Columbia, one year of tuition is $6,200 . At the University of Washington, one year of tuition is $14,000 .

Thinking about health care, child care, family leave, and tuition for higher education, there are all sorts of reasons for workers, including highly skilled professionals, to leave Washington state and move north. And they have.

From March 2025 until January 2026, British Columbia received more than 2,750 job applications from U.S. doctors, nurse practitioners, nurses and allied health professionals. British Columbia has been aggressively recruiting from our state.
Last summer, former Governor Christine Gregoire asserted that the state government has a spending problem . But the reality for working people is that we have a paucity problem.

We have consistently cut back higher education, child care compensation, K-12 education, and care for developmentally disabled Washingtonians, just to name a few. These should be and in previous decades were fully funded as public goods and services.

Indeed, Washington needs to compete – not with Alabama and those states and policies still corrupted by Jim Crow and deep and persistent racism, but with 21st century democracies like those in the Nordic countries and just north of us. We don’t need to accelerate the undermining of the working class and further fatten the portfolios of the already wealthy. These wealthy elite have no loyalty to our state. Just ask Jeff Bezos and Howard Schultz.

articles.title: Neighbors told Kaiser Permanente to re-activate its empty storefronts — Now Emma Cakes is bringing a walk-up bake shop to 15th Ave E
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A new walk-up bakery is set to bring fresh life to a long-vacant retail bay along 15th Ave E at Kaiser Permanente’s Capitol Hill campus.

The City of Seattle has issued a construction permit for the tenant improvement buildout of Emma Cakes inside the 440-square-foot storefront at the corner of 15th Ave E and Denny. Rather than operating as a sit-down cafe, the interior will function as a commercial kitchen dedicated to cake production and baking, paired with walk-up service on the sidewalk. Architectural plans call for modifying a front window panel just left of the main entrance to install a self-closing, bifold pickup window.

The storefront marks a brick-and-mortar expansion for baker Emma Lavine , founder of the Normandy Park-born custom cake business. In a 2024 interview , Lavine shared that she began baking as a creative outlet during the pandemic while studying Studio Arts at San Diego State University . After posting cakes on Instagram for fun, demand from friends and classmates turned the hobby into a side hustle. Following graduation, she formed a company and launched the business professionally, crediting the disciplined, early-morning work ethic she learned watching her father run his own company.
The streamlined footprint is engineered to keep construction and operating overhead low, avoiding major structural and mechanical upgrades typical of a full-service installation.

Until now, Lavine has operated as a one-woman show out of Normandy Park, pitching her custom cakes as edible art for celebrations, ranging from 6-inch two-layer “mini” cakes to 9-inch “extra-large” cakes, alongside add-on cupcakes and pastries. The new storefront gives her a dedicated Capitol Hill cake production facility alongside a street-facing walk-up counter.
The arrival also represents progress in Kaiser Permanente’s push to activate its quiet 15th Ave E streetfront.

As CHS reported in fall 2025 , retail spaces along the block sat empty for years following the pandemic, drawing scrutiny from the citizen Implementation Advisory Committee that oversees the city’s 2018 Major Institution Master Plan for the former Group Health campus.

In response to neighborhood calls to meet its street-activation requirements, Kaiser Permanente brought on hospital retail specialist Health Hospitality Partners and launched a community survey to help shape new food, coffee, and retail offerings.

Commercial listings for the Capitol Hill South Building’s street-level spaces along 15th Ave E show brokers marketing remaining adjacent bays at $28.00 to $30.00 per square foot per year, plus a share of building taxes, insurance, and maintenance.
For now, Emma Cakes is leading the way but there are hopes for more activity to come.
In the meantime, the coming shop will add to this stretch of 15th Ave E’s baked good-ness, joining the nearby location of Bakery Nouveau in serving Capitol Hill’s sweet tooth.
Emma Cakes will open soon at 104 15th Ave E. Learn more at emmacakesseattle.com .

articles.title: Seattle appeals ‘outlier’ $30M jury verdict in deadly CHOP shooting
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The City of Seattle has appealed the “outlier” $30 million jury verdict in the 2020 deadly shooting of Antonio Mays, Jr. at CHOP , arguing the teen was unlikely to have survived even if medics had reached him minutes sooner.
Earlier this month, the city filed its case in the Washington Court of Appeals seeking to overturn the $30.58 million jury verdict awarded to the Mays family.
In its appeal, the city argues the court committed major errors that warrant dismissal in the case or granting a new trial.

In its filing, Seattle contends the plaintiffs failed to prove the city’s alleged three-to-four-minute delay in medical care caused Mays’ death. Under Washington law, plaintiffs must show it was “more likely than not” — greater than 50% odds — that he would have survived. Medical experts testified Mays had at most a 5% to 10% chance of surviving his eight gunshot wounds even with immediate treatment.

The city also argues a misleading verdict form forced the jury to hold Seattle financially responsible for the unknown shooter’s acts, rather than segregating damages or apportioning fault to people in the camp.

The deadly shooting — one of two killings of Black teens in the camp — came early on a Monday morning amid a night of drive-by shooting fears around the protest zone. Mays was shot inside a stolen Jeep Cherokee that had been reported driving at high speeds through the streets around the CHOP camp. The teen died as camp security and medic volunteers worked to save him while Seattle Police and Seattle Fire refused to enter the protest area.
Mays’s 14-year-old companion in the vehicle survived but suffered a brain injury.
The shooting was a final straw as Seattle Police were ordered to storm the protest encampments and clear the area two days later.

Seattle is also challenging a jury instruction that directed a verdict of negligence for Seattle Fire units failing to meet at a disputed rendezvous site, preventing medics from arguing they reasonably avoided a transport vehicle carrying an armed man on its roof.

Evidence presented during the trial by the Oshan & Associates law firm representing the family revealed new details of the confusion within the camp on the deadly night and how SPD failed to enter the zone until hours after the shooting. That evidence helped foil a city defense that Mays was committing a felony crime at the time of his slaying.
The $30.58 million verdict brought the total damages against the city across major CHOP lawsuits to $44.1 million.
In March , the city said it was planning to seek a new trial — or appeal the verdict.

Similar lawsuits were settled by the city before trials began. In 2022 , the city agreed on a $500,000 settlement in the suit brought by Oshan & Associates over the death in the shooting of 19-year-old Lorenzo Anderson on the edge of CHOP. In 2023 , it reached a $3.6 million accord with businesses and property owners over the protest zone. Last year , the city settled its largest CHOP case so far as it reached a $10 million settlement with 50 plaintiffs harmed by the SPD’s flawed response to the 2020 Black Lives Matter and CHOP protests.

Evan Oshan of Oshan & Associates, the lawyer representing the Mays family, was also preparing a case for Robert West who was 14 at the time he suffered injuries that left him permanently disabled in the same CHOP shooting.

Since the verdict, new information has been unearthed about the deady night at CHOP including an account from a previously unknown witness and video evidence that marks the killing as an execution-style shooting after a night of drive-by panic around the protest zone.
No suspects in the June 29th, 2020 killing have been publicly identified. SPD says the investigation of the Mays Jr. killing remains an open case.

articles.title: Wilson says council’s 10-hour budget amendment blitz leaves future $58M hole — These Capitol Hill priorities made the cut
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: The Seattle City Council’s Select Budget Committee spent nearly 10 hours Monday debating and voting on amendments to the proposed 2027–2028 city budget in a convoluted push to tap extra funding as members restored cash for programs they champion and their district priorities amid Mayor Katie Wilson’s effort to wipe away a looming deficit by slowing expensive undertakings like police hiring.

“The proposal that passed the Select Budget Committee increases spending from the General Fund by a net of $36 million in 2027, $31 million of which is one-time. This decreases to a net increase of $14.7 million in 2028, $7.1 million of which is one-time. This means that there is over $20 million of Council-proposed spending in 2027 that is not funded in 2028,” Wilson said in a statement.

“I made difficult trade-offs in my budget not for the sake of accounting, but to prioritize major investments in the areas of greatest need, like a $37 million investment to rapidly expand shelter and bring more people inside,” Wilson said. “The City’s ability to align resources behind these key strategies at the scale that will make a felt impact on affordability and livability for people in Seattle will require new resources.”
“Achieving a sustainable budget is about laying a foundation that creates space for our most important work,” Wilson concluded.

The budget with the council’s amendments relies on $41 million in “one-time” funding for ongoing expenses, creating a projected $58 million deficit in 2029 once those funds expire, according to the mayor.
Monday, budget chair Dan Strauss , said his math added up to a balanced ledger, saying the package the council was working on including the one-time funding.balances the budget through 2030.

Led by Strauss, the council worked all day Monday through the contested budget amendments that had been pulled from the consent package, alongside individual councilmember amendments. Rather than splitting deliberations across multiple days, the committee pushed through the full slate of remaining amendments in a single day ahead of final committee and full council votes later in the week.

Capitol Hill-specific items dotted the day including a 6–3 rejection of the bid by Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck to place a $400,000 proviso on Seattle Police Department surveillance funding that would have withheld camera expansion money until the department implemented three Office of Inspector General audit recommendations — requiring case numbers and justifications for viewing CCTV footage and searching license plate databases, and setting retention and monitoring rules for privately owned cameras.

Opponents included Council President Joy Hollingsworth, Public Safety Chair Bob Kettle , and Strauss. Meanwhile, the committee voted 7–2 to adopt Kettle’s companion proviso governing $4.1 million for the Real-Time Crime Center and CCTV program to encourage continued executive-legislative collaboration.

Beyond the surveillance debate, the committee approved several targeted Capitol Hill and District 3 investments sponsored by Hollingsworth. Following a standalone roll-call vote, members passed a $400,000 traffic safety proviso reserving funds for traffic-calming improvements on 15th Ave on Capitol Hill, along E Madison in Madison Park, and in Leschi, alongside a $50,000 proviso supporting hot meals and outreach aid in Cal Anderson Park .

Additional neighborhood priorities — including $5 million for an anti-displacement rental housing project, $500,000 for tenant services, and $75,000 (rising to $100,000 ongoing) for the legacy Umoja Fest — cleared the committee without individual opposition as part of the broader consent package.

The council will meet as a committee again on Thursday for final votes on the amended 2027 budget and 2028 endorsement resolution, preparing the entire package for a final passage on Friday. You can review the budget documents for that session here .

articles.title: Washington’s Trans Sports Ban Seemed Poised for a Lawsuit. It’s Getting One.
articles.author: Megan Burbank
paras: If Initiative 638, which Washington voters passed with 56 percent of the vote, goes into effect in December, it will ban trans girls from playing on youth sports teams at public schools—and require all girl student-athletes to prove their biological sex. That’s only if it survives the lawsuit filed by the ACLU of Washington, gender equality advocacy group Legal Voice, and the statewide teacher’s union Washington Education Association.

Three days after the initiative results were certified, the groups filed a suit seeking emergency relief to keep it from going into effect on December 3. According to the lawsuit, the ballot measure—which only applies to girls’ sports and trans athletes—would violate multiple provisions of the state constitution. By focusing only on girls’ sports, advocates argue, it would violate the state’s Equal Rights Amendment, and imposing sex verification requirements would violate student privacy, which is also protected under the state constitution.
If I-638 does go into effect, it would put an abrupt end to Washington’s nearly 20-year history of trans-inclusive school sports.

“This new requirement is in direct conflict with the state’s paramount duty to educate our children without discrimination,” said Janie White, president of the Washington Education Association (WEA), which represents 90,000 educators in the state and signed onto the lawsuit, in a news release. “Washington educators are committed to fair and welcoming schools where all students can thrive.”

While the measure focuses on youth sports, Legal Voice policy director Alizeh Bhojani said the threat reflects a much larger ongoing attack on transgender people. “This is definitely part of a broader pattern to push trans people out of public life,” she said, citing bathroom bills and ongoing conservative efforts to constrain access to gender-affirming care.

Opposition to the measure has picked up steam since its passage: Last week, the Seattle Public Schools board of directors voted in support of the district legally challenging the law, something Mayor Katie Wilson cosigned on social media, writing, “I support the Board’s decision and its commitment to creating inclusive learning environments where every student has the opportunity to reach their full potential.”

Last Friday, Attorney General Nick Brown announced that to avoid a conflict of interest, he was bringing in an outside law firm to defend the measure in court. (In true Seattle-is-a-small-town fashion, Pacifica Law Group, the firm taking on the case, also happens to employ former Mayor Jenny Durkan.) The office of the attorney general has advocated on behalf of transgender Washingtonians, and, according to Brown, “We will not and cannot abandon that work.”

Defending the measure may be a challenge given its vague language around enforcement, and the complications it raises in light of the state’s privacy and equal rights policies as well as existing protections for transgender Washingtonians. According to the original language of the initiative , the sex verification requirement for girls who want to play school sports would come from “leveraging the existing physical examination process to verify biological sex.”

But as it’s currently written, the standard sports physical form used statewide under the purview of the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association (WIAA) does not address biological sex at all, just physical attributes and conditions that might make playing sports unsafe for some kids. Noting a cardiovascular or musculoskeletal condition, for example, is a matter of a student’s physical health and safety. Examining and reporting their biological sex is not. The initiative makes no effort to address this mismatch. Another step would need to be introduced into the sports physical process to address biological sex. The ballot measure doesn’t clarify how this would happen, or how it would need to be implemented for students who’ve already obtained a sports physical for the school year.

In fact, the initiative’s Tim Eyman-esque proponent, Brian Heywood, has pushed the idea that the sports physical is an obvious method of determining biological sex, despite its total absence from the form. Advocates fighting the law say this lack of clarity is a huge problem and that it’s predicated on ideas about trans athletes that just aren’t borne out by science.
While anti-trans activists have argued that transgender athletes have an unfair advantage in girls’ sports, the reality doesn’t square with those talking points.

According to a scientific literature review published in Frontiers of Sport and Active Living , there is little data to back this up: “The disproportionate focus on the relatively small portion of the population who are trans seems based on the belief that cis men, who cannot succeed in sports among other cis men, would choose to misidentify as trans women to gain an advantage in sports against cis women,” writes author DJ Oberlin. “However, there are no legitimate cases of this occurring. An individual’s sex does not determine their success or failure at any athletic event despite the high level of competition.”

According to Aidan Key, who advocated for Washington’s trans-inclusive school sports policy when it was first introduced in 2007, educators and rule-making organizations have noted “no distinguishable difference” in athletic performance between trans and cis student athletes. “So this idea that trans girls are going to be dominating girls’ sports is not happening,” he says.

Advocates say this crusade for “fairness” would threaten all girls who play sports and violate the state’s Equal Rights Amendments, because the law’s sex verification would impose a new administrative burden on certain, but not all students and their families—one that isn’t medically necessary, isn’t adequately explained in the language of the initiative, and may not even be covered by insurance. “This is going to be very chaotic for school districts to implement, because we have no clue how they’re going to do that,” said the ACLU’s Adrien Leavitt.
And it’s unclear how girls will have to prove their sex.

“Will that require new medical appointments?” said Legal Voice’s Bhojani. “If it’s not medically necessary, will that be covered by insurance? If a family opts for hormone or genetic testing, that’s going to be even more costly and inconvenient and a delay.”

On Tuesday, the Seattle Times reported that WIAA would be updating its policies to align with I-638 by the measure’s implementation date, December 3. Girls participating in winter sports would need to confirm their biological sex by that date. Bhojani said she hoped an injunction blocking the measure would be granted before then.

articles.title: Pop Loser: A Big Week for Phoebe Bridgers, Grammy Nominations (If You Even Care), and Wake Up, Babe! Bruce Springsteen Said Something Horny Again
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: Welcome back to Pop Loser! This week, Phoebe Bridgers had a big week, extending her tour, playing SNL, and receiving seven Grammy nominations. Bruce Springsteen said something really horny at MOMA on Thursday night. Plus, my emotional support record—Tiger Trap’s 1993 self-titled album—is finally getting a reissue.

This week in Strangerland, Julianne Bell attended Syd’s Beard tour last week, which she described as “sexy, intimate, self-assured, and sweet.” And oh my god, did you see XOË on Noise Complaint last week!? As I wrote in our November print issue, they truly are the best band you’ve never heard.

The Lost Tour is coming back to the Pacific Northwest. Last week, Phoebe Bridgers announced that she will be extending the tour into 2027, adding a date in Portland, as well as Spokane, this coming February. Even though I saw her perform in Seattle last month, these shows are tempting to me because Oregon-based ambient artist Grouper will be opening (ahh!)

It was a big week for Bridgers, who also performed the raucous “ Bobby ” and the heart-wrenching “ Still Standing ” on Saturday Night Live . Both songs felt deeply intimate and provided the masses a rare peek into her phone-free tour . It was also announced on Monday that her album Lost Weekend was nominated for seven Grammy Awards, including Album of the Year.

Speaking of Grammy nominations , here are some highlights (if you even care). Raye received the most overall noms (eleven total), tying with Beyoncé’s record for the most nominations for a female artist in one year. Kanye West’s critically ignored (for good reasons) Bully was controversially nominated for Best Rap Album. Polka-dot math-rock creatures Angine de Poitrine are up for Best New Artist (and I’d love to see them win). Plus, my boyfriend John Cale earned his first Grammy nomination for “House,” his collaboration with Charli xcx.

Wake up, babe! Bruce Springsteen said something horny again. “One of the great pleasures on the Jersey Shore in 1975 was night swimming, preferably naked with someone you wanted to have sex with,” Springsteen said on Thursday night during an address at the 18th Annual Film Benefit held at the Museum of Modern Art. “Steven Spielberg fucked that up,” he continued, speaking of Jaws. “He fucked it up good. Over the years, I asked myself, ‘Why would a nice man like that—why would he do that?’”

A Pop Loser Update: The Edge has broken his silence on Elf 2. As I reported last week, comedian and actor Andy Richter claimed the U2 guitarist had written a sequel to the contemporary holiday classic, and on CBS Sunday Morning , The Edge addressed the rumors. “It’s an outrage for someone to suggest that I would write a script. I wrote a treatment—it’s a different thing—for my own amusement,” he clarified. He went on to explain that, on multiple occasions, he’s woken up in the middle of the night with a complete movie outline running through his head—proving that he is exactly as strange as you’d expect a man who calls himself “The Edge” to be. Sorry, but I have more U2-related news: Dolly Parton’s last recorded song, which happens to be a duet with U2, has been released . This is all I’ll say on the matter.

articles.title: Chef Edouardo Jordan Opens Ice Cream Shop in Ravenna
articles.author: Meg van Huygen
paras: In the summer, a cheery little ice cream shop opened in Seattle’s Ravenna neighborhood, inside a banana-yellow space on NE 65th St. Serving hard-scooped ice cream with complimentary blue sprinkles, Raindrop Creamery focuses on Southern-style flavor profiles like sweet potato latte, banana pudding, and sweet corn and blackberry. There’s also a pantry section for take-home packaged goods, as well as display coolers full of canned drinks, ice cream pints, and frozen housemade soup and stock. The window reads, “Raindrop Creamery: small-batch ice cream with a big chance of Sprinkles!” What it doesn’t advertise is the name of its owner. It’s Chef Edouardo Jordan.

*** Longtime Ravennans and sharp-eyed ice cream fans will notice that Raindrop Creamery occupies the former JuneBaby space—or part of it. They’ll probably remember Jordan’s name too. In the late 2010s, Jordan was the chef-owner of two massively acclaimed Ravenna restaurants, Salare and JuneBaby. For a while, his name was regularly woven into verses with PNW culinary heavyweights like Thierry Rautureau and Tom Douglas. Jordan was honored by national publications from Food & Wine to the New York Times , and Eater Seattle dubbed him 2015’s Chef of the Year. There was usually a line down the block at both Salare and JuneBaby just to make a reservation.

But no locally published story about Jordan can be told without mentioning the sexual misconduct that 15 women accused him of committing. In June 2021, Seattle Times reporters Jackie Varriano and Asia Fields published an extensively researched report based on interviews with dozens of people, both accusers and witnesses, whose claims ranged from Jordan sending them raunchy texts and commenting on their breasts to grabbing their butt or crotch and kissing them without consent. Some were his employees at the time of the incidents, while others were his coworkers, friends, or acquaintances. The incidents occurred between 2012 and 2019. No criminal charges were filed.
On the day the Seattle Times story broke, both of Jordan’s restaurants suffered major staff walkouts, leading to their closures several weeks later.

Although Jordan initially denied remembering the incidents alleged in the June 2021 Seattle Times story, he published an “unequivocal” apology on Instagram on July 3, 2021, which was also published by the Seattle Times . In part, Jordan’s statement read: “While I am deeply ashamed of my past behavior, I am immensely proud and grateful of what my team and I have accomplished over the years. It was solely up to me to exemplify the protective leadership that they could trust. And I failed them.“

In 2023, after JuneBaby closed permanently, the two-time James Beard Award winner continued using the space next door as the prep kitchen for his Food with Roots pantry goods business, selling items like pimento cheese and Haitian pikliz at farmers markets, food events, and grocery stores. This July, he added ice cream and reopened the space to the public.

*** On the Raindrop Creamery website, it’s not immediately obvious who owns the shop, although there are clues. A link to the website for Food with Roots appears at the top of the home page. Jordan’s name also appears in the Raindrop Creamery site’s FAQ (although most of the way down the page), and he is pictured in a group photo on the Our Story page.

Jordan co-owns Raindrop Creamery with his partner, Sitara Marin, a licensed mental health counselor and practicing psychotherapist who works in the shop part-time. Marin also handles HR for Raindrop Creamery’s employees.

The ice cream shop hasn’t done much marketing so far, other than some light posts on the socials. In September 2026, Jordan appeared on KIRO-FM’s Gee and Ursula Show to talk about the store’s opening, and Puget Sound Business Journal covered Raindrop’s debut in October 2026. Both KIRO and PSBJ subsequently faced online backlash for giving Jordan a platform, including criticism from Seattle-based chef and author J. Kenji López-Alt on a PSBJ Instagram post. López-Alt’s comment was later deleted.

At the shop, when asked by The Stranger if he was trying to stay under the radar with Raindrop, Jordan chuckled and replied, “I don’t know if I’ve ever stayed under the radar. There’s nothing to hide, honestly.” ***

It seems that Jordan’s been trying to stage a comeback for a minute. Notably, he reopened JuneBaby in January 2022 , just a few months after the Seattle Times story ran—possibly testing the waters for a return to public life. It shuttered for good in December 2023. Marin also mentions My Truth, My Story , Jordan’s self-produced 12-part “docuseries” published on YouTube in October 2025, wherein Jordan tells his side of the sexual misconduct story. Although the series does feature some mea culpas by Jordan, he also spends considerable time defending himself. At the new scoop shop, the question of whether Jordan will reoffend is still close to the surface. He and Marin say they’ve solved for that. “All of our employees go through training,” Marin said. “We have an operations manual. I take care of the front-of-house employees, so they’ve been through anti-harassment training and all that.” She added that, as a licensed mental health counselor, she is a mandatory reporter.

Marin said they are willing to face criticism in person too. “We’re happy to have the conversation with anyone who wants to come in here,” she said. “There have been customers who have been like ‘Hmm, well, I don’t know,’ and we don’t mind talking with them about what happened. We get it.”

“The biggest word that I can circle among everything that happened is accountability ,” Jordan said. “Everyone’s like ‘You’re not accountable. You haven’t been accountable. What’s your accountability? What have you done to be accountable?’

“You know, I’m accountable for my mistakes. I’m accountable for the things that I’ve participated in and actually was actively involved in. But I’m never gonna fall on the sword that everyone else is putting up. There’s some bad words that people use. You know, ‘You’re a rapist! You’re an N-word! You should die!’ I’m like ‘What? You have no clue what even occurred.’”

He reiterates that he’s apologized. “I had this conversation with Jackie [Varriano] like two years after her article came out. So, there’s a link [on my blog] that you can go to, and it’s not stuck to the front page. I had it stuck [to my Instagram profile] there for a year and a half or two and continually got people berating me, trolling me, and so after a while, it’s like ‘Why am I sitting here, just getting punched?’ So I took it out and put it directly into my blog .” He points out that he did initially post the apology publicly on his Instagram, until he was harassed for it.
“So how long do I have to walk around with a scarlet letter on my head? Forever, right?” ***

Let’s zoom out for a sec. While Jordan is one of the best-known local examples, the nation’s vanity-driven, booze-soaked, hedonism-based restaurantscape sees a disproportionately high rate of sexual harassment and assault cases when compared to other industries—alongside wage theft , tax fraud , verbal abuse , permitting skulduggery , serving alcohol to minors , unpaid employees , and a jambalaya of other ignominies . Seattle’s seen its share of these in 2026 alone. And, of course, sexual misconduct cases are almost certainly the most hateable among them. Because this happens a lot, and with chef-owners especially, there’s sort of an established field guide of don’ts and dos. When dirty deeds are revealed and the press spotlight snaps on, the public apology is a crucial first step. It must be done swiftly and correctly. Sincere apologies and subsequent atonement are real art forms, and they can be powerful and even exculpatory when done right. Sadly, most people fuck them up.
Five years out from the Seattle Times exposé, no one can deny that Jordan has confessed to and apologized for his sexual misconduct. But it still hasn’t stuck. Why?

To some, his apologies have rung disingenuous, exacerbated by his initial denial of the assaults and his habit of defending his past actions in the same breath. Others haven’t taken kindly to Jordan deciding that he’s back on the scene, whether with or without their forgiveness. And for many, especially survivors of sexual assault, an apology alone was never going to cut it in the first place. Some are just not interested in forgiving him. For others, it’s the actions that follow the apology that’d ostensibly win them back.

Jordan seems to believe he’s done the work it takes to atone. Has he, though, enough to be welcomed back? And is he sincere, or is it all lip service, as some local chefs and Redditors have implied ? That’s for the ice-cream-eating public to decide.
