articles.title: Slog AM: More System Outages, Dems Nominate Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, We Should Convert Trump’s Ballroom into a Center for the History of American Activism
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: If you are reading AM right now , then thank your lucky stars because nothing else, it seems, is there to protect you from or help you through this recent rash of systemwide computer crashes. On November12: Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams, and Microsoft 365 went dark. On November 13: the Federal Aviation Administration’s telecommunication systems began bugging out; same with systems at Claude and Workday . On November 16: Chase Banks’ online services crashed. Yesterday: outages occurred at the National Security Agency and Apple . Which systems will crash today? How long will this crisis continue? Now might be a good time to consult the prepper in you.

Today will not be cold enough for me. Some people you can find “in da club,” but I’m one of those vampires who like to be found in temperatures between 30 to 35. Put some thick clouds all in there, almost no sunlight, and a long night, and I’ll reach a state of bliss that’s obtained by the likes of Barnabas Collins . Expect a high of 45 today.

Democrats have nominated center-left Rep. Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker of the House . This opens the way for him to become the first Black American to hold that position. Jeffries, however, received a lot of resistance from the side of the party that’s progressive and wanted a House leader with greater distance from corporate cash and interests. Nevertheless, his run for speaker received support from the Mayor of America, Zohran Mamdani , and progressive superstar Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez .

The most terrifying Black Mirror episode is without a doubt “ Metalhead .” It does not have much of a story: A woman, Bella (Maxine Peake), runs from an activated robot dog that has no other purpose than to kill her. In one scene, Bella climbs up a tree. The robot dog can’t do the same, so it shuts down and waits for her to return to the ground. Bella is stuck in the worst way. If she returns to the land, she is done. If she falls asleep and falls from the branches, she is dead. The robot dog does not care how long it’s going to take; it knows she can’t stay up there, up in the branches, forever. All it has to do is wait for the inevitable.

What’s this? The Seattle Police Department “unveiled a four-legged robot” for the Arson/Bomb squad. This mean machine can climb stairs (hopefully not a tree) and “navigate challenging [terrains].” And, along with a 360-degree camera, it has a “robotic arm that can grasp, lift, carry, and move objects.” The robot is called SPOT, and was purchased with a grant from the Federal Emergency Management Agency that was approved by the Seattle City Council, people who evidently never watched Black Mirror ’s most nightmarish, disturbing, distressing episode, “Metalheads.”

Are you surprised? When a Black reporter for NBC News, Yamiche Alcindor, asked Trump if he was too “focused on construction projects,” such as his ballroom, instead of on issues that concerned “the country’s airline systems,” he told her, without batting an eye: “Listen to me. I know you don’t see dirt… [And] you never notice broken windows, obviously, from where you come.” For those not in the know, Trump was referring to the broken windows theory , which asserts that broken windows signify crime, bad and lazy people, and general disorder in an urban area. Blacks often lived in these neighborhoods, and the theory was used to explode police budgets and impose zero-tolerance policing . Trump is, and will always be, exactly what he is: a racist.

What to do with Trump’s ballroom when he’s history? I recommend transforming it into a center that celebrates what Howard Zinn famously called A People’s History of the United States . Do not destroy the ballroom. Repurpose it. Make it not about him but we the people. The heroes of AIM (American Indian Movement), hardcore labor leaders, civil rights activists, militant Suffragettes, Stonewall’s freedom fighters—all of that and more, non-stop, day in and day out, in the ballroom. And best of all, this cultural center for radical and democratic America will dwarf the White House, and, on some nights, its tall windows will be filled with the colors of the rainbow.

Big science news? Maybe not . A team of Japanese scientists attached to the University of Tokyo, the Institute of Science Tokyo, and Kindai University made this impressive claim: They created the first hybrid plant-animal cells in the history of life as we know it. (Life has been around for some 4 billion years.) The scientists called this biological remix “planimal” cells. But hold your horses. These cells aren’t really hybrids because the animal cells actually repress key features of the plant cells during fusion. So, basically, what they’ve developed in their lab are, at best, interesting animal cells. Am I getting this right? Nevertheless, this story, by way of the neologism “planimal,” offers us an opportunity to refer to one of the most numinous lines in all of English literature: “It darkles, (tinct, tint) all this our funnaminal world.”

Deep in the mists and thickets of James Joyce’s practically unreadable novel (or whatever that thing is called), Finnegans Wake , you will find the sentence “It darkles, (tinct, tint) all this our funnaminal world.” Ignore the “tinct, tint” and instead focus on the word “funnaminal.” The word is like a dub tune. It doubles/echoes/ghosts these other words: phenomenal, fundamental, animal, and fun. From the portmanteau “darkles” (dark and sparkles) emerges the phenomenal human, human animal, the fundamental human, and the fun animal. But here is the thing that Joyce’s genius reveals: We know the human has an appearance (phenomenal), we know the human is a part of the tree of life (the animal), we also know that the human is made of matter, of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and other heavy elements that were forged in stars that, when reaching the end of a sequence, exploded and had their nuclear fused contents spread across vast areas of space (fundamental).

Let’s end AM with a track by Juan Atkins, “Starlight.” His death, which occurred on the last day of October, still demands more recognition. This Black man practically invented techno. Yes! Named it. Developed it. Expanded it. One day we will give this loss the gravity it deserves.

articles.title: Where to eat, shop and hike on Whidbey Island
articles.author: Rachel Belle
paras: Falling in love with a place can echo falling in love with a person; the thrill of beauty, discovery and fun buzzing alongside feelings of ease and contentment. I suspect there are also some sort of invisible geographical pheromones at play. I felt it the first time I touched down in Mexico City, instantly smitten with this brand-new place despite only seeing rows of tall jacaranda trees, in full violet bloom, rushing by the window of my Uber as we sped away from the airport. I hadn’t stepped foot on a city street, eaten a taco, seen a lucha libre match or visited the Frida Kahlo museum, and yet: “I could live here!” I thought. Instant connection.

I feel a similarly deep connection to Whidbey Island, a place I visit several times a year. Riding a ferry always feels like being on vacation, and this one sails a brief 20 minutes from Mukilteo, which gives me just enough time to do my “mall walking” around and around and around the main cabin.

Once we’re docked on the Whidbey side, my Little House on the Prairie life is activated . Summertime has us picking blackberries, sour cherries, peaches and strawberries, that may get baked into a clafouti or sliced up for shortcake. We’re paddling out to drop crab pots in the morning and, by late afternoon, cleaning and steaming Dungeness in the backyard. We’re digging for bait clams at Double Bluff Beach, churning homemade ice cream, jumping off the dock into Deer Lake – life has never been so wholesome!

But if wearing a bonnet and churning butter isn’t your idea of a good weekend, here are some of my other favorite things to do and eat on Whidbey Island – a very easy day trip from Seattle. My mini guide starts in south Whidbey and makes its way up north to Oak Harbor.

Yarn shop up front, speakeasy cocktail bar in the back – co-owner Marsha Owen hand-dyes the yarn and her husband Matt Owen shakes the craft cocktails. The bar is cozy, only 21 seats, with an ornate copper tin ceiling, dark wood and enough nautical touches to conjure up images of Brandy, the barmaid from The Looking Glass song🎵 But my life, my love, and my lady is the sea! 🎵 Though you’re more likely to see a group of knitters sipping on a vintage-inspired cocktail than a crew of sailors throwing back whiskey and wine.

Marsha was an overworked, burnt-out postal worker and Matt was a graphic designer when they decided to take a risk and try something new. “We always wanted to have a cocktail bar,” Marsha told me. I don’t wanna braaaaaaaaaag, but I was the first reporter in the country to cover this quirky little spot when it opened in 2022. My radio story found its way to The Associated Press wire and drew visitors from across the country!

My favorite of their cocktails, the Whidbey Bramble, is only available over the summer months. Matt uses spirits from Whidbey Island Distillery, located just up the road – their blackberry liqueur and Bunker Rye is shaken with a little lemon juice and muddled blackberries and mint, poured over crushed ice and garnished with a bouquet of fresh mint and a toothpick strung with blackberries.

Tucked into the seaside village of Langley, the cutest and quaintest town that you absolutely must visit, is a ramen shop that can compete with some of the bowls of noodles I slurped in Japan. Chef/owner Denis Zimmermann, who grew up in Tokyo, quit his advertising career to open Ultra House, named after the Japanese superhero Ultraman, and recreated the steaming bowls of tonkatsu ramen he grew up eating. His pork bone broth is rich and creamy, the noodles bouncy, and some of the colorfully garnished bowls are drizzled with his black garlic oil. There are also bowls of chicken, shrimp and vegan ramen, crispy-bottomed gyoza and rice bowls. Perfect for a chilly island day.

A fairly easy hike with a start-to-finish payoff, it’s nothing but wide-open Puget Sound and Cascade Mountains views as you amble along the bluff. The full hike is a loop that eventually takes you down to the beach, and you’ll walk along the sandy shoreline back to the trailhead. But when I’m short on time or energy, I simply turn around at the end of the bluff and hike back the way I came. There are two starting points: Leaving from the beach parking lot gets you to the bluff faster, but I prefer to take the Prairie Overlook trailhead by the Sunnyside Cemetery, past fields of alfalfa, bushes dotted with rosehips and views of electric green fields.

Whidbey has two adorable little shopping district villages, Langley to the south and Coupeville to the north (the latter was the filming location for the 1998 film Practical Magic!) and they are each home to a wonderful, women-owned specialty food and home store with a tempting cheese case; everything you need to execute a cute-ass picnic. Both shops are well stocked with tinned fish, fancy chocolate bars and every artisan spread, pickle, mustard, potato chip, cracker and vinegar you could ever dream of, all encased in irresistible, artsy-fartsy packaging. Bayleaf also makes fresh-to-order sandwiches and other deli items.
I am forever grateful to Bayleaf for introducing me to my favorite butter of all time and for stocking my cookbook!

Look! Another wholesome Whidbey activity! You’ve never been to a drive-in movie? Gee whiz! Pack up the station wagon with blankets and shake a tail feather before these vintage theaters are gone for good. Blue Fox opened in 1959 and is one of five remaining drive-in theaters in Washington state. They’re open year-round – seven days a week in summer and Friday through Sunday through the colder months. And it might be the best movie deal around – $6.50 for adults, $1 for kids five to ten years old and free for the littlest ones. They also have an affordable snack bar and when I interviewed the owner back in 2019, I was surprised to learn that their pizza is homemade:

“We make our own crust, we grate the cheese fresh and make our own sauce,” Darrell Bratt said. “Better food for a drive-in because I do like food and I like food that tastes good! We try to keep our prices very low because I come from a family of seven, I have four children, I know what it’s like to entertain a large family."

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.author: Keza MacDonald
paras: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre
Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI?

In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it.

For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building.

articles.title: ‘They want silence’: how the film NAZA is shaking Israel
articles.author: Michael Segalov
paras: The documentary has triggered fierce backlash, but by exposing the army’s conduct in Gaza it’s proved impossible to ignore

It was on Yom Kippur this year that Nadav Weiman first sensed the documentary NAZA was having a significant impact in Israel – despite the fact that back in September, when the Jewish festival fell, barely a handful of Israelis had seen the film.

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and will stream for free on its website in early December, depicts 24 army intelligence officers interviewed anonymously on rooftops across Tel Aviv. They talk about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza over the past three years, and the secret signoff system employed by Israel’s military. More than 1.5 million people have already seen it in cinemas and its Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have picked up a roster of prestigious awards. The film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel but has not been screened there yet, amid a severe backlash.

articles.title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback
articles.author: Andrew Lawrence
paras: After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement

I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech.

Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs.

articles.title: ‘Worst decision in cinema history’: Guardian readers shaken and stirred by the casting of Robert Pattinson as Bond
articles.author: Guardian readers
paras: ‘Deliciously dark’! ‘Not sexy enough’! Opinion is split on whether the star of Twilight and The Batman is the right choice to play 007. Here’s what some of you thought

So it’s official, Robert Pattinson will be James Bond. The long-awaited announcement of who would be stepping into 007’s tuxedo came as a surprise, and has divided opinion, judging by the more than 700 responses the Guardian received to a callout on the topic.
Readers were split on whether bosses at the franchise’s owner Amazon were right to give the role to the star of Twilight, Tenet and The Batman. Here are some of their views.

articles.title: AI helps uncover critical flaw in ubiquitous internet software
articles.author:
<name>Doug Jacobson, University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/doug-jacobson-809162"/>
paras: If you checked your bank balance, booked a flight or ordered groceries online today, there is a good chance your request was handled by a computer program written in Java.

For nearly three decades, the Java programming language has been one of the quiet workhorses of the internet. While most people rarely interact with it directly on their phones or laptops, it sits at the heart of most large, behind-the-scenes server applications that power modern business, finance and government.

That ubiquity is why a new critical security alert from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency drew the attention of technology teams worldwide. Security researchers uncovered a severe flaw, dubbed Java4Shell , in a core Java component. If left unpatched, the bug could allow an attacker to trick a vulnerable server into executing malicious code.

As a cybersecurity researcher who studies how large-scale software systems fail and how to defend them, I see this discovery as both a standard call to action for system administrators and another milestone in a broader shift: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how hidden flaws in critical software are discovered.
To understand the vulnerability, it helps to know why Java became so popular in the first place.

Normally, software must be tailored to the specific computer hardware and operating system it runs on. Java solved that headache with a clever piece of software called the Java Virtual Machine . It is essentially a program that runs other programs. Software developers write their Java application once, and the Java Virtual Machine provides a uniform foundation on top of a server’s operating system, running that application regardless of the underlying machine.

In addition to running the application, the Java Virtual Machine provides a standardized set of code for everyday tasks, such as reading files, managing network connections and formatting incoming data.

One of those routine tasks is Base64 encoding . Computers often need to send complex data, such as images, attachments or authentication tokens, over text-based internet protocols. Because raw binary data can be corrupted in transit, systems convert it into a string of standard text characters using Base64. When a Java server receives that string, its Base64 library decodes it back into its original form so the application can use it.

The newly discovered vulnerability resides in the Base64 decoding library in Oracle’s implementation of the Java Virtual Machine. This means that any application using this version of the Java Virtual Machine is at risk.

According to technical analysis of the flaw, a carefully crafted piece of malformed Base64 data can overwhelm the library’s processing, allowing an attacker to break out of normal boundaries, execute unauthorized commands and potentially gain control of the server.

If this sounds familiar, it follows a pattern seen recently with a high-profile PHP vulnerability , another foundational web language. Like the PHP vulnerability, this Java flaw was uncovered by cybersecurity firm Calif using AI tools to search for vulnerabilities.

Calif officials said the company alerted the governments of the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Britain, and major tech companies, including Google and Microsoft, before the Java vulnerability became public. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency then issued its alert, urging organizations to immediately patch the flaw .

Historically, identifying subtle memory or parsing errors buried deep within millions of lines of mature code required months of painstaking manual review by human experts. Today, security researchers are pairing AI tools with traditional code analysis to systematically probe software libraries for edge cases that humans might overlook for years.
Whenever a critical vulnerability affects a foundational piece of software, headlines can sound alarmist. In reality, there are several reasons to maintain perspective while still acting quickly.

First, the good news is that a responsible security researcher discovered and privately reported this flaw, giving people who maintain software time to develop and release a fix before attackers could widely exploit it.
Second, everyday users do not need to panic about their personal devices. This is an issue affecting enterprise applications and cloud infrastructure, not home laptops, smartphones or tablets.

Third, even on vulnerable servers, exploiting this bug in the real world is not always straightforward. Most modern web systems do not expose raw Java decoders directly to the open internet. Instead, incoming traffic typically passes through several types of software – firewalls , load balancers and web proxies – that inspect, sanitize or reject malformed data before it reaches the underlying Java application.

Still, “harder to exploit” does not mean impossible, especially for internal systems or custom applications that pass user-supplied bits of information, called tokens , directly to Java’s decoder. As with any foundational infrastructure repair, the best defense is straightforward: promptly applying the latest security updates.
As AI accelerates the discovery of long-hidden software flaws, keeping the digital infrastructure patched remains one of the most effective cybersecurity practices.

articles.title: Florida’s flooding déjà vu is a sign of things to come – so, who is most at risk and how can they prepare?
articles.author:
<name>Smitha Rao, Associate Professor of Social Work, The Ohio State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/smitha-rao-1432926"/>
paras: Floodwater filled the streets and crept into homes across Florida’s Atlantic coast as an intense storm dumped more than a foot of rain in 24 hours starting Nov. 17, 2026. The deluge followed extreme downpours in parts of the region less than three weeks earlier , and forecasters warned of more rain still to come .
As people in Fort Lauderdale watched the water rise in their already saturated yards, it may have felt like déjà vu.
In April 2023, more than 25 inches of rain fell in Fort Lauderdale in 24 hours. Even hurricanes rarely drop that much rain in one area that fast. Residents could do little to stop the flooding.
Studies show that as global temperatures rise, more people will be at risk from such destructive flooding – including in areas that rarely faced extreme flooding in the past.

In many of these communities, the people at greatest risk of harm from flash flooding are low-wage workers , older adults and other vulnerable residents who live in low-lying areas and who have few resources to protect their properties and themselves.

I study the impact of extreme weather on vulnerable communities as an associate professor of social work . To limit the damage, communities need to know who is at risk and how they can be better prepared.
The Florida storms offer a view into the risks ahead as temperatures rise . These risks are especially high as the effects of a strong 2026-27 El Niño set in .

A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture , leading to stronger downpours. The resulting deluges can be devastating. These events are expected to increase in frequency and intensity in many regions as greenhouse gas emissions from human activities continue to heat up the planet .
Recent disasters show how the risk of flash flooding is expanding beyond areas traditionally considered at risk .
To plan for extreme weather, it’s crucial for community leaders and residents to know where the risks are highest and who might not be prepared .

Low-lying areas with poorly planned development , lack of investment in protective infrastructure and the lingering effects of historic disinvestment and discrimination are often at higher risk. So are low-income communities with tight budgets that can’t afford protective measures like upgraded levees or stormwater systems and can’t recover from damage quickly.

When older adults live in these flood-prone areas , they are at even higher risk. Older adults have a higher likelihood of having health needs or some form of disability that could affect their ability to leave quickly during a disaster. They are also more likely to be socially isolated , which may mean they don’t hear timely information or have help to evacuate or quick access to resources for recovering.

My colleagues and I have examined how prepared people are for disasters of any kind across the U.S. – flooding, tornadoes, hurricanes and others – and how housing security played a role. The numbers are sobering.

Overall, we found in a 2023 study that 57% of the population, among 29,070 housing units surveyed nationwide, reported they were not prepared with food, water, emergency funds and transportation in case disaster struck. We found that households facing housing insecurity – those behind on their payments for rent, mortgage or utilities – were less prepared for disasters than others, even when the occupants had similar incomes and education.

People who are struggling to meet day-to-day needs often don’t have the ability and resources to plan for everyday events, let alone for disasters. Our research has shown that households with children, households led by women, and low-income households were less prepared than others for disasters.

Renting adds additional challenges. In the U.S., lower-income families often depend on the rental market . They tend to move more frequently, and since they don’t own the property, they often can’t make upgrades for safety. And landlords might not prioritize those risks that seem rare but carry costs.
The most effective way to address these challenges is through solutions that are tailored to the community.

That can involve investing in infrastructure , including state-funded priorities such as drainage systems, large-scale flood prevention measures and strengthening the power grid , as well as ensuring that people have access to safe and affordable housing . Some communities and federal agencies have bought out properties that frequently flood and changed zoning rules to prevent more people from moving into harm’s way.
Raising community awareness about climate change and extreme weather risks is also crucial, especially among those most at risk , such as older adults and other socially marginalized groups .

If people understand the risks, know how to prepare their homes, know how to plan for emergencies , know whom to contact for help, and have stronger systems of care, they’re more likely to be prepared when disasters strike.
I believe the most successful efforts are those that bring at-risk communities into planning discussions .

For example, in Columbus, Ohio, the city partnered with the Central Ohio Area Agency on Aging, Age Friendly Innovation Center and my team to improve disaster preparedness among older residents . We worked with older adults in affordable housing communities and the human service professionals who support them to help design action plans for communities with special needs in the event of an emergency. The tool kit we created can help social service providers prepare low-income residents for extreme weather.

Our team is now working with service providers nationwide to document best practices, identify gaps and ensure residents are better prepared for climate- and weather-related emergencies in the future.
This article updates a story published April 27, 2023 , about flood risk in South Florida.

articles.title: A convincing vegan meat alternative needs both taste and texture – here’s how food scientists manufacture them
articles.author:
<name>Rohit Singh, Postdoctoral Researcher in Food Materials Science, West Virginia University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/rohit-singh-2776405"/>
paras: This Thanksgiving, you may sit down to a table laden with mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, vegetables and a golden-brown turkey. And, if you have any vegetarians or vegans in your family, you may even see a plant-based meat alternative. But how do food scientists make something taste and look similar to turkey entirely from plants?

Plant-based meat alternatives have become an increasingly prominent part of the food industry , driven partly by concerns about the sustainability of conventional meat production and the search for additional protein sources. One life-cycle assessment found that plant-based patties had a 77% lower climate impact than the Brazilian beef patties examined, although the results varied depending on the production systems and environmental measures considered.

But making a convincing meat alternative is not as simple as replacing animal protein with plant protein. How do you turn ingredients from peas, soybeans or wheat into something that looks, tastes and feels like meat?

When people think about protein, foods such as chicken, beef, eggs and milk often come to mind. However, plants are also important sources of protein . Soybeans, peas, wheat, lentils and other legumes contain proteins that can be extracted and used in food products.

Soy and pea proteins are widely used in plant-based meat alternatives . Wheat protein, or gluten , can also contribute to their structure and chewy texture. Researchers are also exploring other sources, including fava beans and mung beans, to expand the range of ingredients available.

But plant proteins behave differently. Some absorb more water, while others bind fat or form structures that hold ingredients together. These properties influence how a food feels when you bite into it. Choosing a protein therefore involves understanding how it behaves during processing, not just its nutritional value.

Think about biting into a piece of roasted turkey breast. Its texture comes from the arrangement of muscle fibers , along with connective tissue, water and fat. Together, these components create firmness, juiciness and the chewing experience you associate with meat.

Plant proteins have structures that are different from animal muscle proteins. Mixing pea or soy protein with water does not automatically create meatlike fibers. Food scientists use processing methods that organize these proteins into structures that more closely resemble muscle.

Flavor matters, too. Fat adds juiciness and carries flavor compounds, while heating creates familiar roasted and savory aromas. A convincing meat alternative must bring together the right ingredients and processing conditions to reproduce these qualities.

One widely used method is extrusion . Protein-rich ingredients are mixed with water and pushed through a machine that applies heat and pressure while mixing the material. These forces unfold the proteins and help them interact.

As the mixture cools, the proteins form aligned, fibrous structures that resemble some features of meat. High-moisture extrusion uses more water during processing, which produces fibrous products with a more meatlike texture.

The final structure depends on factors such as the protein source, moisture content, temperature and processing conditions. These factors influence how proteins interact and form the fibrous structures found in plant-based meat alternatives .

Manufacturers can also add fats, starches, flavorings and other ingredients to improve the eating experience. Small changes in formulation or processing can make a considerable difference, affecting whether a product is firmer, softer, chewier or better at retaining moisture.
Another emerging approach is 3D food printing. Like a conventional 3D printer , a food printer builds an object layer by layer, depositing edible materials according to a digital design.

Our research explores protein-based food inks: mixtures designed to flow through a printer nozzle and hold their shape once deposited. Developing the right formulation is challenging because the material must be fluid enough to print but still firm enough to retain its shape. Researchers are applying similar principles to explore printing plant-based meat alternatives.

Instead of relying only on conventional manufacturing methods, 3D printing could allow researchers to control how different ingredients are arranged. For example, you could potentially deposit protein-rich materials and fat-containing ingredients in specific patterns to create different structures and textures.

Recent research on the 3D-printing of plant-protein-based meat analogs highlights how the formulation of the food ink and printing conditions influence how accurately a product can be printed and whether it holds its shape. However, a printed product that looks like meat must still deliver the expected texture, flavor and eating experience.

Plant-based meat alternatives are not necessarily intended to replace traditional meat. They offer consumers additional choices, but making them appealing, affordable and consistent remains a challenge. Scientists continue to study how proteins, ingredients and processing work together to create the textures and flavors people enjoy.

The next time you see a plant-based burger or turkey alternative, remember that making it involves much more than replacing animal protein with plant protein. Technologies such as extrusion and 3D food printing are helping scientists explore new ways to turn plant ingredients into meatlike foods.

articles.title: Today’s Thanksgiving holiday was invented amid the Civil War to unite a divided country
articles.author:
<name>Samira Mehta, Professor of Women and Gender Studies & Jewish Studies, University of Colorado Boulder</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/samira-mehta-1109963"/>
paras: It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England’s first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God’s providence.

Children learn the story as if it were history – and as though Americans have commemorated Thanksgiving the same way ever since. The only existing eyewitness account of this event does not, however, say much about what was eaten. A slightly later account of the 1621 harvest mentions seasonal food such as venison, corn – and, yes, turkeys.

The idea of a straight line connecting that “first Thanksgiving ” to Thanksgivings today is, in fact, an American myth. It is a story created in the 19th century to unify a nation and long used to assimilate new immigrants into it.

The Pilgrims and Puritans, who started arriving in Massachusetts shortly afterward, regularly held fasts and feasts . On fast days, the community atoned for sins they believed they had committed. On feast days, they gave thanks to God. Some governors of colonies – and later, states – declared fall holidays of thanksgiving , but did not coordinate with each other.

The Thanksgiving that we know, with the traditional recipes and the close connection to the Pilgrims, was largely the creation of one woman: Sarah Josepha Hale , who was born in New Hampshire in 1788. In the 1830s she became the editor of Godey’s Lady’s’ Book , which had the largest circulation of any U.S. magazine before the Civil War.

Godey’s included clothing patterns, recipes, articles on home management, essays on educating children, recipes and fiction. Hale believed that the woman was the heart of the home and responsible for creating an upstanding, God-fearing, wholesome family.

She was also deeply committed to her young country and believed that homemakers could help create its national identity. According to historian Elizabeth Pleck , Hale began publishing editorials calling for a national Thanksgiving , along with instructions for what the day could look like.

Godey’s taught readers how to celebrate the day, with recipes for seasonal food such as turkey and cranberry sauce. The centerpiece of the table was the pies, which featured elaborate pastry decorations: the Mayflower or a cornucopia, created out of pie crust. The full table was a celebration of “women’s work,” at a time when the Industrial Revolution was shifting the economy toward factories and other business , making the importance of unpaid domestic labor less obvious.

Hale’s idea of Thanksgiving also emphasized returning to loved ones, as those factories were drawing many workers away from home. She saw it as a day to tell family stories – and the story of the nation, starting with the first Thanksgiving.

Hale petitioned five presidents to declare Thanksgiving a national holiday. Abraham Lincoln finally took her up on it, hoping that a national holiday emphasizing the country’s origin story would prove uniting during the Civil War.

Northern women sent pies to the families of soldiers and turkeys to the men at the front. Pleck notes that abolitionist Sojourner Truth went door to door , collecting funds to provide Thanksgiving dinners to African American troops.

The holiday caught on gradually . Given the Protestant origins of early Americans’ feast and fast days, Catholics were slow to embrace it. Given its association with Lincoln and the war, the South was also late to adopt it. And given the day’s emphasis on family, it was less celebrated on the frontier, where single men dominated.

Wherever Thanksgiving was celebrated, however, Godey’s Lady’s Book taught Americans how to celebrate it. The magazine’s op-eds connected the holiday menu and the past, using the Pilgrims’ courage to inspire 19th-century Americans dealing with massive changes in their own lives: war, industrialization, urbanization and the frontier.
Before long, Thanksgiving was also seen as a way to assimilate immigrants.

This vision was, in part, popularized by political cartoonist Thomas Nast . “ Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner ,” which appeared in Harper’s Weekly in 1869, depicted Americans from any number of races and ethnicities in their national dress: men, women and children sitting as equals around a dinner table, with portraits of presidents on the wall, while Uncle Sam carved a turkey.

The image suggested that immigrants could be incorporated into the nation – and formerly enslaved people, too. It was printed just one year after the 14th Amendment granted citizenship to anyone born in the U.S. and four years after the 13th Amendment formally ended slavery.

Nast’s image contrasted sharply to another cartoon, also called “ Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner ,” that G.F. Keller drew for the San Francisco Wasp eight years later. Keller’s disheveled and entirely male collection of diners each ate their own national food, or offensive stereotypes thereof, suggesting immigrants could never truly become American.

But many Americans believed they could – although they demanded most immigrants give up their “Old World ways” and take on customs of their new country. Thanksgiving was part of the engine of that assimilation.

In the early 20th century, public schools taught about Thanksgiving and sent children home with recipe cards so that their parents could cook the same kinds of recipes Hale had popularized in the previous century. Schools framed the Pilgrims and their first Thanksgiving as the spiritual, if not literal, ancestors of all Americans: the first “immigrants.” They didn’t dwell on how the Pilgrims’ arrival looked more like colonization than immigration.

The holiday became a way to include newcomers in the national myth. By the 1920s, in fact, Thanksgiving was the most celebrated holiday in public schools . Pleck quotes one Jewish immigrant reflecting on his childhood and saying the Pilgrims were a way to connect “us offspring of Jewish immigrants – our own exiled fathers who had crossed the seas – and the traditions of Protestant America .” Students acted out the first Thanksgiving and were told they belonged to a “nation of immigrants.”

While some immigrant parents rejected the holiday, others embraced it, with spins to make it their own. Many served a turkey surrounded by the celebratory dishes of their own cultures. For Jews, the early 1900s invention of Crisco as a nondairy butter substitute allowed them to create a truly “American” Thanksgiving and dessert, without violating kosher rules against mixing meat and milk.

The fact that most families celebrate at home allowed immigrants and their children to take part in the national culture, while still expressing their own. During my own New England childhood, an Indian neighbor had my mother’s fairly classic cranberry relish, and by the end of the weekend she’d worked out a cranberry chutney with Indian spices. When we had Thankgiving dinner with my parents’ friends the Stalzmans, who were Jewish, matzah ball soup was the opening course.

At times, the idea of the Pilgrims arriving on the Mayflower has been used to exclude – to imply that only Americans whose literal ancestors came over on the ship , and other white Protestants like them, truly belong. Yet on the holiday in their memory, generations of new Americans affirmed that they, too, belonged.

articles.title: How the US power rivalry with Russia and China is turning outer space into the next battlefront
articles.author:
<name>Scott Shackelford, Professor of Business Law and Ethics, Indiana University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/scott-shackelford-335009"/>
paras: U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink recently confirmed that the United States has weapons deployed in Earth’s orbit . To date, the U.S. Space Force , the space service branch of the U.S. armed forces, has provided relatively few details about what these weapons are or what they can do except that they are what Meink called “on-orbit space control weapons.”

Meink’s announcement is significant, but not necessarily because the U.S. is the first country to place weapons in orbit. For years, the U.S., Russia and China have accused each other of developing and testing such capabilities, although none has publicly acknowledged deploying space weapons – until now.

We are scholars of space law and governance , and our research illustrates the challenges of uniting diverse groups to establish norms related to the use of resources, safety zones and conflict prevention in new domains such as space. Without better communication and deeper coordination between the world’s space powers, we could witness the beginning of a space arms race.
In 1981, the United Nations added the Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space, known as PAROS , to its agenda.
More than four decades of diplomatic efforts under PAROS have produced meager results , though there was a United Nations agreement in 2024 that made progress on reducing threats.

Despite many countries’ proclamations supporting space arms control , no multilateral treaty banning weapons in space has been adopted. With global arms control generally in retreat , and the apparent lack of political will among the three major space powers, efforts to control space weapons have reached an impasse.
The question increasingly is not whether an arms race in space can be prevented, but how it will be managed.
The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 , to which all major space powers are parties, is often described by scholars, practitioners and policymakers as the constitution of outer space.

Article IV of the treaty remains the only legally binding international provision specifically regulating weapons in outer space. The article prohibits countries from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit around Earth. It also imposes a broader prohibition on military activities on the Moon and other celestial bodies, including establishing military bases, testing weapons and conducting military maneuvers.

However, the article does not prohibit conventional weapons in Earth’s orbit. That omission is significant. The treaty can be understood as implicitly permitting what it does not prohibit : the placement of such weapons in orbit.

China has used these ambiguities as cover for its own space weaponization efforts. In a 2007 test, China destroyed one of its own satellites while in orbit, and it has recently deployed a mysterious space plane .

China, nonetheless, reacted critically to the recent U.S. weapons announcement. In September 2026, it urged Washington to stop expanding its military presence in space . That same month, Russia renewed calls for the demilitarization of outer space .

Both countries have long advocated stronger international restrictions on space weapons. Russia and China twice jointly proposed a treaty prohibiting the placement of weapons in outer space . The U.S. opposed the proposals in 2014, pointing to their failure to also cover important ground-based, anti-satellite weapons.
But Russian and Chinese declarations in favor of keeping weapons out of space sit uneasily alongside their own activities.

In 2020, U.S. Space Command, part of the Defense Department, accused Russia of testing a space-based anti-satellite weapon after an orbiting Russian satellite released a projectile. Russia said the spacecraft was performing an inspection mission.
In 2024, the United States said Russia had launched another satellite, Cosmos 2576, which it assessed to be a “counter space” weapon capable of attacking other satellites .

China has similarly demonstrated increasingly sophisticated operations in orbit. Five Chinese spacecraft conducted satellite flybys in 2024, an exercise that a senior U.S. Space Force officer later described as practicing “dogfighting in space.”

None of this proves that every suspicious Russian or Chinese spacecraft is a weapon. Many technologies used for servicing, inspection and maneuvering around satellites are inherently dual-use. But it does put Moscow’s and Beijing’s calls to keep weapons out of space in perspective.

It also illustrates the security threat now taking shape. Washington can point to Russian and Chinese activities to justify its own weapons. Moscow and Beijing can now point to acknowledged U.S. weapons to help justify their actions, which could result in a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Space has been part of warfare for decades. The 1991 Gulf War has sometimes been called the first “space war” because of the unprecedented role satellites played in navigation, communications, intelligence and targeting. But satellites primarily supported military operations taking place on the ground.
That distinction has gradually eroded. NATO formally recognized space as a military theater in 2019 .
Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine then demonstrated something different, in which the very definition of a weapon was challenged.

Hours before Russian troops crossed the border, a cyberattack disrupted the U.S. satellite network Viasat , in what was dubbed by commentators as the first “ space-cyber war .” Space-based services were no longer merely supporting military operations but were themselves deliberately targeted as part of a military campaign.

The acknowledgment of weapons in orbit represents another step in that evolution. Space assets are transitioning from systems that primarily support warfare in other domains to systems that can be weapons, targets and participants in combat and are often replete with vulnerabilities that could be exploited by an adversary.

That does not mean future space warfare will resemble Star Wars dogfights or Starfleet armadas taking on Borg cubes. But the emerging battlefield is likely to be much more complicated. Satellites can be disrupted through jamming and spoofing, disabled through cyberattacks, approached or manipulated by other spacecraft, attacked from Earth or potentially attacked by weapons already in orbit.

This makes the connection between space and cyberspace particularly important. A country seeking to neutralize an adversary’s satellites may have several options, ranging from a cyberattack or electronic interference to physically damaging it. At the same time, space-based critical infrastructure has never been more vital to the functioning of the global economy.
Military strategy therefore has to adapt not merely to warfare in space but to warfare across an increasingly interconnected space-cyber nexus .

The important question is no longer whether space will become militarized. It has been militarized for decades. Nor is it even whether states will develop weapons capable of affecting objects in space. Several already have done so.

The new question is how nations manage a strategic environment in which weapons are openly deployed in orbit, satellites are increasingly being targeted, and attacks can move between the space and cyber domains.
Public acknowledgment may itself have strategic consequences.

The U.S. Space Force argues that revealing the existence of its orbital weapons can strengthen deterrence by making adversaries aware that it possesses capabilities with which to respond. But transparency can also accelerate competition.
Russia and China can now point to U.S. weapons to justify deploying their own. The same logic and its consequences animated debates during the Cold War .

Forty-five years after the United Nations began debating the prevention of an arms race in outer space, that arms race increasingly looks less like something to prevent than something governments must learn to manage.

articles.title: The stunning transformation of the Southern Democratic Party, in one lifetime
articles.author:
<name>Gibbs Knotts, Professor of Political Science, Coastal Carolina University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/gibbs-knotts-1402490"/>
paras: Two of the biggest surprises of the 2026 election cycle were Democratic U.S. Senate victories in the Deep South. In addition to Annie Andrews’ victory in South Carolina , Scott Colom won a close contest in Mississippi , a place that historian James Cobb called “ The Most Southern Place on Earth .”

Colom is not Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator. Two Black Republicans represented the state during Reconstruction , when state legislatures still selected U.S. senators. But Colom is the state’s first popularly elected Black U.S. senator . He is also the first Democrat that Mississippians have sent to the Senate since 1982 .

It is tempting to read this change using a familiar political science term: party realignment . But as political scientists who study political campaigns and Southern politics , we see an equally important transformation in the electorate – the people who can cast votes.

Simply put, the Democratic Party in the South was transformed from a party that defended white supremacy and Black disenfranchisement into one in which Black voters became a central constituency . The Democrats who held Mississippi’s Senate seats for the majority of the 20th century were chosen by an electorate built to exclude Black citizens. Colom was elected by a dramatically different electorate and represents a very different Democratic Party.
To understand the magnitude of the change in Mississippi, it helps to look at the Democrats who came before Colom, what they stood for, and the political power they wielded.

For a brief period after the Civil War, Black Mississippians exercised real political power. They were a majority of the state’s population and, with the right to vote, helped elect the state Legislature that sent Hiram Revels to the U.S. Senate in 1870 and Blanche Bruce in 1875 , both of them Black.

That period did not last. White Democrats regained control of Mississippi government in the 1870s, aided by political violence, intimidation and electoral fraud . In 1890, the state adopted a new constitution that used poll taxes, literacy tests and other restrictions to systematically disfranchise Black voters. Two years after the new constitution took effect, the percentage of Black men registered to vote had fallen to just 5.4 percent .

The result fundamentally changed Mississippi politics. For the next several generations, the Democratic Party dominated a political system in which most Black Mississippians had little meaningful voice. Republican electoral victories were rare. One newspaper in 1963 claimed that the election of Lewis McAllister to the state House was the party’s first win in 43 years. Without a competitive general election, winning the Democratic primary often meant winning office, and the politicians who emerged from a one-party system made possible by Black disenfranchisement became some of the most powerful political figures in the state’s history.

What happened in Mississippi reflected a broader pattern across the South. In 1949, political scientist V.O. Key published his seminal study of the region, “ Southern Politics in State and Nation .” Key argued that the solid Democratic South rested on systematic disenfranchisement of Black voters.

The one-party system helped keep Black Southerners out of political power while allowing white Southern politicians to present a unified front against efforts to dismantle segregation and expand Black voting rights, particularly when those efforts came from the federal government. Mississippi was among the clearest examples of that system.

Before Colom, the last Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi was John Stennis in 1982 . He first won election in 1947, filling the seat of Theodore Bilbo , who had won reelection in 1946 after a campaign in which he urged white Mississippians to keep Black voters away from the polls . Stennis won a 1947 special election with 52,068 votes in a state of 2.2 million people. He held that seat for 41 years.

Throughout much of his career, Stennis was an ardent segregationist . In 1956, he was one of 101 members of Congress from the South who signed what was called the “ Southern Manifesto .” In that statement, these lawmakers denounced the Supreme Court’s decision in Brown v. Board of Education , in which the justices ruled that the “separate but equal” standards of racial segregation were unconstitutional; Stennis and the other signatories pledged resistance to school desegregation.
Later in his Senate career, Stennis was the only Southern Democrat who voted to oppose the creation of a national holiday honoring Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.

Stennis’ Senate colleague for much of his tenure, Mississippi Democrat James Eastland , was an equally staunch defender of segregation. A cotton planter from the Mississippi Delta, he was appointed to the Senate in 1941 and won the seat outright in 1942 . He remained in the Senate until 1978.

The day after the Supreme Court handed down its 1954 decision in Brown v. Board of Education, Eastland was quoted saying , “the South will not abide by nor obey this legislative decision by a political court.”

Recent attention has understandably focused on Stennis, the last Democrat to represent Mississippi in the Senate. When Colom takes office, he will occupy the Senate seat once held by Eastland and Democrat James Vardaman , who said that “if it is necessary every Negro in the state will be lynched; it will be done to maintain white supremacy.”

One-party rule also gave Mississippi’s senators unusual power. With little electoral competition, they could remain in office for decades. In a Senate where seniority mattered, longevity translated into influence.

Eastland, for example, chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee for more than two decades, giving him enormous influence over civil rights legislation. During his chairmanship of the powerful committee, that committee became known as “the graveyard of civil rights legislation,” according to the Senate’s website.

The Voting Rights Act of 1965 helped dismantle the electoral system that had sustained these men in office. Before it, fewer than 10% of Black Mississippians were even registered to vote . Within a few short years, a majority were.

Black voters increasingly aligned with the Democratic Party as its national leaders embraced civil rights, even while many Democratic officeholders in Mississippi continued to defend segregation. That meant Black voters sometimes supported incumbent white segregationists . The party’s voters changed faster than many of its candidates did.

The 1978 election for the seat Colom will hold illustrates how complicated that transition could be. After Eastland retired, Charles Evers, brother of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, ran as an independent and drew nearly a quarter of the vote . His candidacy split the traditionally Democratic vote, helping Republican Thad Cochran win with a mere plurality.
By the 21st century, white Mississippians overwhelmingly supported Republican candidates, and Republican dominance had replaced the old Democratic dominance in most statewide elections.
That pattern made Colom’s victory all the more striking . He won with overwhelming support from Black voters while also attracting enough white voters to build a winning statewide coalition.

The contrast with Mississippi’s old Democratic coalition could hardly be sharper. The Democratic Party of Vardaman, Bilbo, Eastland and Stennis maintained its power in part by keeping Black Mississippians away from the ballot box with violence and Jim Crow laws.
When Colom is sworn in, Revels’ old seat will, for the first time, be held by a Black senator directly elected by Mississippi voters.

articles.title: Op-Ed: It's Time to Reconnect Fremont and Grapple with the Barrier Aurora Avenue Creates
articles.author: Ankur Dhoot
paras: In 2021, SDOT began studying improvements to Aurora Avenue with funding from WSDOT and King County Metro. In 2022 , the Washington State Legislature allocated $50 million for a demonstration project in the Licton Springs section of Aurora Avenue. The state wanted design completed by fall 2023 , and for construction to begin in spring 2024. In other words, the state wanted the city to take action quickly.
The city opted to continue studying the entire corridor instead and, in 2024 , the intent to fund $50 million for Aurora was dropped from the state budget.

In the five years since the study began, not much has changed. The most meaningful near-term improvement is likely a signalized crossing of Aurora and N 137th St. Otherwise , a few turn restrictions, hardened centerlines, and repainted crosswalks are all SDOT has to show for five years of work.

The proposed alternatives in the long term corridor study leave much to be desired . The agency's current estimate for when the study will be completed and construction on larger capital projects will begin is now 2031 - a full decade after the study began. (Of course, this assumes funding will be available then.)

We need to build momentum for change along Aurora. Trust is lost when planning and studies take a decade without meaningful near-term changes. Reconnect Fremont is a demonstration project to overcome the existing inertia, rebuild trust with the community, and make people reimagine Aurora as more than a highway bisecting their neighborhood.

Aurora Avenue is classified as an Urban Village Main through Fremont. According to SDOT’s Streets Illustrated guidelines: “ while Urban Village Main Streets must accommodate the movement of people and goods through the Urban Center or Village, the design of these streets encourages slower speeds and clearly communicates that walking, bicycling and transit access are prioritized.”

If you’ve ever traveled along this section of Aurora, you know that walking, bicycling, and transit access are not prioritized. A concrete barrier runs down the center, and there are no street level crossings. For vehicles, this section of Aurora is an uninterrupted freeway. For everybody else, it’s a physical barrier.

Different stretches along Aurora have different problems. The most obvious issue in the Fremont stretch currently is high speeds (speed limits were reduced in other sections of Aurora in 2021, but not in Fremont), no accessible crossings, and a dearth of E Line stops. From N 68th Street near Green Lake to the Aurora tunnel, there is not a single street level crossing.

The E Line is the highest ridership bus line in Washington State. But the only E Line stop in Fremont is at N 46th Street. The nearest northbound stop is at N 65th St, more than a mile away. The nearest southbound stop is at Lynn Street, more than 1.5 miles away. There is only a single E Line stop in a 2.5-mile stretch through one of the densest neighborhoods in North Seattle!

It doesn’t have to be this way. Reconnect Fremont proposes a series of concrete improvements that will restore east-west connectivity, improve transit access, and build momentum for the entire Aurora corridor through near-term action.

As the densest part of Fremont, the desire for an E Line stop at N 38th Street is over a decade old . King County Metro would like to build a stop here, provided that the city and state install a safe street level crossing.

The current walk from the sole E Line stop at N 46th Street to the Fremont core is 20+ minutes . An E Line stop and street level crossing at N 38th Street will provide improved access to the Lower Fremont commercial district, as well as the increasing density along Stone Way.

There is currently a pedestrian overpass at Aurora and N 41st Street, just a block from the B.F. Day Elementary School. In 2025, SDOT completed a seismic retrofit of this bridge at a cost of more than $2 million , despite the schools in the area having previously requested a street level crossing be installed at this location.

The enrollment area of B.F. Elementary School spans both sides of Aurora. Parents with strollers or kids with bikes have an unnecessarily difficult experience trying to cross Aurora using the inaccessible overpass.

As the Seattle School Traffic Safety Committee said , “A safe, pleasant, at-grade crossing will reunite a neighborhood with the happy add-on of making the commercial spaces along Aurora more accessible for all.”

The first neighborhood greenway in Seattle was the Wallingford Neighborhood Greenway (now rebranded a Healthy Street ). It connects to Hamilton International Middle School, Lincoln High School, the Wallingford Playfield, and the Wallingford commercial district along N 45th Street. The Healthy Street currently ends at Stone Way, but there is an opportunity to extend it further west.

The enrollment areas of Hamilton International Middle School and Lincoln High School cross Aurora. The Upper Fremont Neighborhood Center will add density a few blocks west as well, and a 71-unit supportive housing facility already exists on the west side of Aurora and N Motor Place.

A street level, signalized crossing of N Motor Place can extend Seattle’s first Neighborhood Greenway, provide a safe bike connection for kids getting to school, and connect the increasing density in Upper Fremont with the existing commercial district in Wallingford.

The lone E Line stop in Fremont is at N 46th Street and serves more than a thousand riders per day. It is also a transfer point to Route 44 which connects to U District and Ballard. The bus stop is surrounded by on- and off-ramps and high speed traffic.

It is a common sight to see someone hop the jersey barrier to catch the E Line on the other side of Aurora Avenue. A street level, signalized crossing at N 46th Street would provide safe and convenient access to this bus stop.

In 2023, Chief Seattle Club opened the Goldfinch building at Aurora and N 48th Street. In 2026, DESC opened Clover Place at Aurora and N 49th. Plans are currently underway for a multi-purpose athletic field at Woodland Park near Aurora and N 50th Street to serve Lincoln High School. The Woodland Park Zoo (which draws over a million visitors per year) is a few blocks from Aurora and N 50th.

There is significant demand for an E Line stop and street level crossing at Aurora and N 50th. The Woodland Park Zoo has expressed support for such improvements, as have the Friends Of Lower Woodland Park and the neighbors in the area.

There is currently no all ages and abilities bike route from the Burke-Gilman Trail in Fremont connecting to Woodland Park and Green Lake. Most people take Stone Way N, which contains a door-zone bike lane going north and no bike facilities at all going south. Stone Way N is an arterial listed on the High Injury Network , although it got some safety improvements in 2026 as a result of advocacy from Ballard Fremont Green Streets.

Woodland Park Avenue was listed on the original 2014 Bicycle Master Plan and the 2024 Seattle Transportation Plan as a neighborhood greenway. Building this greenway would provide a much-needed connection between the Burke-Gilman Trail and Woodland Park. The main challenges are the crossings of the arterials – Bridge Way N , N 46th Street, and Green Lake Way N – but some improvements are already on the way.

In 2016, a Neighborhood Street Fund application was submitted for crossing improvements at N 46th Street and Green Lake Way N, but was not chosen for funding. In 2026, one of the projects selected in the D4 District Project Fund was an enhanced pedestrian crossing of Bridge Way N at the Woodland Park Avenue intersection.

With the aforementioned signalized crossing of Aurora Avenue and N Motor Place, we can build the desired bike route between the Burke-Gilman Trail and Woodland Park without having to wait for future improvements at N 46th Street and Green Lake Way N. How? In 2022, the Route 44 TPMC built a crossing of Linden Ave N and N 46th . By making a greenway on Linden Avenue N at N Motor Place, we have the connection to Woodland Park. Linden Avenue N is already a proposed greenway in the Seattle Transportation Plan, and this connection would also create a safe route to the Upper Fremont Neighborhood Center .

The Aurora Reimagined Coalition has hosted two walks for Reconnect Fremont . Reconnect Fremont has been presented to the Fremont Neighborhood Council, Seattle School Traffic Safety Committee, Seattle Pedestrian Advisory Board, and Lincoln High School PTSA, and is endorsed by a broad coalition of organizations, such as the Cascade Bicycle Club, Amalgamated Transit Union 587, Ballard Fremont Green Streets, the Downtown Emergency Service Center, the Fremont Chamber of Commerce, the Fremont Neighborhood Council, the Transit Rider’s Union Bus and Transit Service Committee, and Transportation Choices Coalition.
Reconnect Fremont has also received letters of support from Cascade Bicycle Club , Friends of Lower Woodland Park , and the Woodland Park Zoo , and has strong support from state lawmakers.
Let our leaders and decision makers know that you want to Reconnect Fremont - sign the Action Network campaign !

articles.title: Old timers say goodbye to Mediterranean Express as Garlic Crush set to close on Broadway
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Mediterranean Kitchen Express, Mediterranean Express, Garlic Crush — However you knew it, the affordable falafel and shawarma joint has been part of its stretch of Broadway since the 90s.
Thursday will be the restaurant’s final day :

To our amazing Seattle guests, thank you. Thank you for every visit, every shared meal, every kind word, and every memory we’ve made together. Being part of the Capitol Hill community has meant so much to us, and we will truly miss seeing your familiar faces!
You can still visit its sibling locations in Bellevue, Issaquah, Redmond, Woodinville, and, soon, Kirkland, ownership says.

The closure ends a long history of Lebanese flavors on the block. Long run as Mediterranean Express, Maher “Matt” Jabbour took over his brother’s joint in 2019 to make it part of his growing Garlic Crush chain. Not a lot changed and the favorites including excellent garlic fries continued on even as big chain neighbors like Chipotle moved in next door.

The closure comes as the Harvard Market shopping center changed hands earlier this year. CHS reported here as the two-level center and parking facility at Broadway and Pike has been acquired for $14.2 million by San Diego-based developer Tourmaline Capital .
Thanks Google Maps for a few images through the years

While other closures have left blank spots in the center’s street-level mix including the 2024 closure of the block’s AT&T store, improvements and increase security under the new ownership has helped reduce disorder and public safety concerns around the QFC -anchored shopping center.
Meanwhile, some long-term food and drink tenants at Harvard Square have continued to thrive. Ooink is celebrating ten years of craft ramen above Pike and Broadway this year.
As for the Garlic Crush space, a check of city paperwork didn’t reveal any immediate plans for the soon to be emptied restaurant space.
Garlic Crush is located at 1417 Broadway and is planning its final day of business on Thursday, November 19th. Learn more at garliccrush.com .

articles.title: King County’s 2027 budget includes plans for a new $4M tiny house village in the Central District
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: King County and the Low-Income Housing Institute are moving forward with plans to open an 80-unit tiny house village in the Central District in early 2027, part of a broader push to expand shelter capacity for both families and individuals living unsheltered.

According to King County Executive Girmay Zahilay’s office, the county is committing $5 million toward the Spruce Street Tiny House Village as part of a larger supplemental budget package aimed at advancing his goal of creating 500 new housing and shelter units within 500 days. While Zahilay announced a $5 million commitment in September, King County Council budget documents for the proposal specify a $4 million appropriation toward the project’s development as the council reviews the 2026–2027 budget proposal ahead of a final vote scheduled for November 24.

The new village will be situated on county-owned land at the vacant southeast corner of the Judge Patricia H. Clark Children and Family Justice Center campus. LIHI, the nonprofit housing developer and shelter operator that manages 18 tiny house villages across the region, will partner with the county to build and operate the site.

This summer, CHS reported on the opening of LIHI’s Belmont Village , a $1.1 million project that created 31 shelter homes on a Capitol Hill lot eventually destined to be built up to a new 120-unit permanent supportive housing facility from the the Downtown Emergency Service Center .

The county investment comes as Mayor Katie Wilson has also made tiny house villages a centerpiece of hoped-for shelter expansion in the city. This spring, the Seattle City Council approved Wilson’s plan for “Shelter Acceleration” that raised legal limits on residents at “transitional encampments” to 150. The bill also allows one “interim use” 250-resident village in the city. The plan has produced only limited progress including 75 new units at a new village in Interbay. Wilson has slowed her shelter goals under 2027 budget planning . In March, the administration framed the delivery of 1,000 shelter units as a single-year objective for 2026. Wilson is now extending that goal through the end of 2027, scheduling 960 total beds to serve an estimated 1,750 people annually across facilities established in 2026 and eight sites slated for 2027.

The county is leading the way on the Spruce Street Tiny House Village funding as it puts its surplus property to use. Just south of Capitol Hill, the county’s $242 million youth jail and justice center opened in the winter of 2020 with 16-cell living halls designed to look like dorms but secured for incarceration with electronic locks and state of the art surveillance systems, new classrooms, and an expanded visitation areas where youth offenders can meet with family and lawyers.

The new tiny village will fill an empty corner on the south of the campus. The area south of the justice center is an ongoing public safety issue for the city where the Wilson administration and the Seattle Police Department have instituted a new approach to street disorder that hasn’t really made a dent in issues at the corner. The blocks in between are happier places including Bailey Gatzert Elementary School and the Washington Hall community venue.

The Central District area has hosted several tiny house villages providing transitional shelter for unhoused residents. Currently, three villages operate in the neighborhood — True Hope Village with 33 units on E Yesler Way, a Low-Income Housing Institute site opened in 2018 on church property for families, couples, and single adults, T.C. Spirit Village with 24 units on 22nd Ave, a LIHI-managed site opened in 2020 at Christ Spirit Church focused on serving Native American, Alaska Native, and Black residents, and Nickelsville Central District on 21st, a resident-governed encampment serving singles, couples, and families.

The neighborhood was home to Seattle’s first officially sanctioned tiny house village that opened in late 2015 on 22nd Ave in partnership with the Lutheran Church of the Good Shepherd before being cleared to make way for Good Shepherd House , an 86-unit permanent supportive housing building that opened in 2024.

Designed as an enhanced shelter rather than a basic encampment, the Spruce Street facility will feature 80 insulated, heated, and lockable tiny houses. According to project plans released by the executive’s office, approximately 30 units will be dedicated to families with children, while the remaining 50 units will serve singles and couples.

Alongside residential units, the site will include a community kitchen, shared gathering space, a children’s play area, hygiene and laundry buildings, and dedicated offices for on-site staff and case managers.

LIHI says that its tiny house village model is intended to serve as a safe, dignified bridge between street homelessness and permanent housing. At existing LIHI villages, on-site case managers assist residents with employment, health services, and housing navigation, helping more than half of exiting households transition into permanent homes in 2025, according to the organization.

Representatives from King County and LIHI have already begun community outreach, presenting site plans to Central District residents at a Squire Park Community Council meeting in October. Pending final budget approval from the King County Council , construction and site preparation are slated to move forward ahead of an anticipated opening in early 2027.
